Article Title: In 2014, a Palm Beach couple paid $9 million for a dated 1955 waterfront house, rebuilt it through an extensive renovation, then sold the Everglades Island estate 11 years later for $25.4 million
Article Text:
Buyer already has land across town

The Thornburghs bought for $9 million

Inside the renovated mansion

Cornelia ‘Cornie’ Thornburgh and her husband, Richard, have sold their renovated lakefront mansion and guest house on Everglades Island in the Intracoastal Waterway, the Palm Beach Post reported.The house at 550 Island Drive was listed at $24.9 million, according to the multiple listing service. The deed, recorded on Jan. 10, 2025, shows a price of $25.4 million. The buyer is 260N Property Limited Partnership, which is registered in Manitoba and uses a mailing address at an office building in Toronto.The buyer is not new to Palm Beach. It owns a four-bedroom house at 260 N. Woods Road in the North End. It paid about $6.28 million for the 1977 house in September 2020. In March 2022, it added the empty lot next door at 254 N. Woods Road for $9.25 million. That lot is about a third of an acre.The house and lot are now on the market together for $22.9 million, the listing service shows. Agent Jim McCann of Premier Estate Properties holds that listing. He also represented the buyer in the Island Drive deal.The Island Drive estate did not sell quickly. The agents, Liza Pulitzer and Whitney McGurk of Brown Harris Stevens, first listed it in April 2023 at $39 million.After several price cuts, its final price landed about $13.6 million below that first asking price.Built in 1955, the mansion sits on about half an acre, with 150 feet of frontage on the canal that separates the island from the Everglades Golf Course. The Thornburghs bought the property in 2014 for $9 million. They felt the mansion needed a gut renovation. “This house was dated and a bit of a wreck. We saw that it was a project, but we also knew it was a special place,” Cornie Thornburgh told the Palm Beach Daily News in 2023.The couple hired architect Jacqueline Albarran of SKA Architect+Planners. Contractor Tim Givens of Tim Givens Building & Remodeling Inc. ran the work. The team changed the layout of the main house a great deal but kept the focus on the water views and the thick mangroves along the golf course. “Not one thing went untouched,” Thornburgh said in the same interview.The Thornburghs went for a massive renovation. The main house now has five bedrooms, four of them on the ground floor, along with a den and access to a two-car garage. The living and dining rooms open to a poolside lanai. The main suite is upstairs and has a balcony facing the gorgeous water.Wide-plank hardwood floors run through the rooms. The vaulted ceilings in limed wood are another highlight. The mansion also has gas fireplaces in the living room and lanai, setting the tone. The kitchen has custom cabinets and high-end appliances. A two-bedroom guest house and cabana building also sit nearby. After the renovations, the couple named the property Pelican Strait. The Palm Beach couple were keen on hosting parties, and their entertaining space can host about 100 people. “We have had parties here for 100 people, and now the house flows well. In so many big houses, you ramble around, but this house is cosy and comfortable when there’s no kids around and it’s just the two of us,” the couple said.The Thornburghs had to downsize, so they moved to a 1920s bungalow at 159 Australian Ave., just east of the police headquarters near Town Hall. They bought the historic home in 2023 from Amy Tarrant for $8.12 million. The 4,436-square-foot home has five bedrooms. The town gave it landmark protection in 2013, and earlier owners won an award from the Preservation Foundation of Palm Beach for restoring it. Elizabeth Woody of Compass Florida represented both sides of that sale.Prior to owning the mansion on Island Drive, the couple owned another landmarked house, a 1923 villa on Golfview Road. Richard Thornburgh, a senior adviser at private-equity firm Corsair Capital LLC, also has ties to New York, but the latest tax rolls list the Island Drive house as their main home.The estate is the seventh house north of the short bridge that links Everglades Island to the rest of town through Island Road. The island runs three-quarters of a mile along the Intracoastal Waterway, in the town’s Estate Section.
Article Summary: Cornelia 'Cornie' Thornburgh and her husband, Richard, have sold their renovated lakefront mansion and guest house on Everglades Island in the Intracoastal Waterway. The house at 550 Island Drive was listed at $24.9 million, according to the multiple listing service. The buyer is 260N Property Limited Partnership, which is registered in Manitoba and uses a mailing address at an office building in Toronto.

Article Title: Prince William launches Amazon partnership to protect Indigenous defenders; partner reaches 110 million hectares, with DiCaprio's video support
Article Text:
Image: Left/Wikipedia/Right/Beautiful World

What Prince William announced at the 2025 United for Wildlife Global Summit in Brazil

Leonardo DiCaprio appeared by surprise video message and urged world leaders to take urgent action

DiCaprio's message gave added profile to its cause (Images: Wikipedia)

Why the Amazon needs protecting: Illegal logging, gold mining, land-grabbing and threats to defenders

How the partnership will work across nine states and shared threat data

What 110 million hectares means, the scale of Indigenous territory reached by the Amazon partnership

In November 2025, Prince William used the stage of the fourth annual United for Wildlife Global Summit in Rio de Janeiro to unveil a new alliance for the people who defend the Brazilian Amazon. The partnership aims to protect Indigenous leaders and nature defenders working across territory covering 110 million hectares. Actor and environmentalist Leonardo DiCaprio added his voice to the occasion through a surprise video message. The initiative arrived days before the United Nations climate conference in Belém, at a time when destruction of the rainforest and violence against its guardians were rising. Here is what it promises.United for Wildlife reported that on Tuesday, 4 November 2025, the Prince of Wales unveiled an ambitious initiative to partner with Indigenous Peoples and nature protectors across the Brazilian Amazon and to strengthen their protection. The strategic partnership brings together The Royal Foundation's United for Wildlife programme, the Coordination of Indigenous Organisations of the Brazilian Amazon, the Podáali Fund, Rainforest Foundation Norway (RFN) and Rewild.In his keynote address, Prince William told the summit audience: "We cannot manage our forests while their protectors live in fear." He added that the initiative means working alongside those who know the land best, strengthening Indigenous-led systems and delivering legal aid and emergency support.The summit had a surprise guest. People reported that DiCaprio, then 50, joined the Prince of Wales, then 43, by video message on 4 November. He told leaders at the meeting that the time to act had come. People also reported that Prince William unveiled a plan to help those striving to protect Indigenous people who are losing their livelihoods to deforestation.The video was also published on DiCaprio's Instagram page, and the Oscar winner said, "Nature is our most powerful solution." DiCaprio was not named as a partner in the initiative. His message gave added profile to its cause.According to United for Wildlife, the Amazon faces a double crisis of accelerating environmental destruction and escalating violence against those who protect it. In 2024, more than 1.7 million hectares of rainforest were cleared, much of it driven by illegal logging, gold mining and land-grabbing.Satellite analysis published in June 2025 by the Monitoring of the Andes Amazon Program, using University of Maryland data, shows how far the damage reached. It found that deforestation across all nine Amazon countries in 2024 was the fifth highest since 2002, a 34 per cent jump from 2023, with Brazil responsible for 54.7 per cent of the total and Bolivia for 27.3 per cent. Fire made 2024 even worse, blazes damaged a record 2.8 million hectares of primary forest, and Brazil and Bolivia accounted for 95 per cent of that damage. Deforestation and fire together affected 4.5 million hectares, the highest combined total ever recorded. The programme noted that agriculture and gold mining drove most deforestation hotspots without major fires.Indigenous communities, whose lands host approximately 27 per cent of the Brazilian Amazon, bear the damage to their livelihoods, ancestral lands and sacred sites. Their stewardship works: United for Wildlife noted that deforestation in Indigenous lands is up to 83 per cent lower than in unprotected areas.The people doing that work face growing danger. In 2023 and 2024, 393 cases of violence against environmental defenders were recorded in Brazil. Indigenous and Afro-descendant communities were disproportionately affected, accounting for around a third of those killed or who disappeared in 2024.According to United for Wildlife, the partnership seeks to break down barriers to the safety of Indigenous leaders across nine states of the Brazilian Amazon. It will prioritise wider access to legal support and an emergency response fund to help people at risk reach safety, whether through emergency evacuation, secure communications, safe houses or humanitarian aid.The partnership will also raise global awareness of Indigenous Peoples' rights and their vital role in protecting the Amazon, and will improve the monitoring of threats through a shared data platform.The scale comes from the Indigenous partner at its centre. United for Wildlife said the Coordination of Indigenous Organisations of the Brazilian Amazon reaches 750,000 Indigenous people across approximately 110 million hectares of Amazon territory.Its Executive Coordinator, Toya Manchineri, told the summit that the safety of those who defend the forests with their own lives must be central to global discussions. For Indigenous peoples, he said, the territory is sacred, a place where the spiritual and the material come together. He described protecting it as a mission inherited from ancestors and invited the world to join the struggle.Doctor Tom Clements, Executive Director of United for Wildlife, said that protecting the land and resources of Indigenous Peoples and local communities is one of the most effective ways to protect nature and fight climate change. He stressed that the initiative is built and led by Indigenous-governed delivery mechanisms, offering a model for how the global community can support nature protectors everywhere.
Article Summary: Prince William unveiled new alliance for people who defend the Brazilian Amazon. Leonardo DiCaprio appeared by surprise video message and urged world leaders to take action. The initiative aims to protect Indigenous leaders and nature defenders. It will prioritise wider access to legal support and an emergency response.

Article Title: Dr. Phil and Robin McGraw bought a Beverly Hills property for $29.8 million in 2010 and completed the mansion a year later; 16 years on, the 16,079-sq-ft estate is listed for $67.5 million
Article Text:
Photo credit (L-R): Getty Images; Realtor.com

A major jump in value

A private resort-like compound

Pool, tennis court and expansive grounds

Dr. Phil McGraw and Robin McGraw are ready to part ways with their lavish Beverly Hills estate, more than a decade after transforming the property into a grand Mediterranean Revival-style mansion. The couple purchased the property for $29.8 million in 2010 and completed the residence a year later after a lengthy construction process. Now, 16 years after acquiring the land, the 16,079-square-foot estate has been listed for $67.5 million, according to Realtor.com. The asking price is more than double the couple’s original purchase cost and reflects the scale, privacy and extensive amenities of the sprawling compound. Set across 2.76 acres in the Beverly Hills Post Office area, the estate combines old-Hollywood glamour with the comforts of a modern luxury retreat. Read more details about their lavish house, as per Realtor.com, here:The property is being marketed by Billy Dolan of Carolwood Estates. If it sells close to the asking price, the transaction could give the McGraws a difference of approximately $37.7 million between their original purchase price and the current listing price. However, that figure does not include the money spent on construction, landscaping, later improvements, maintenance, taxes and selling expenses.According to Realtor.com, the couple bought the property in 2010 and completed the mansion in 2011.The residence was designed by architect Kevin Clark, although the construction process reportedly stretched across seven years. The result is not simply a large family home, but a complete private compound designed for entertaining, relaxation and accommodating guests.The estate includes eight bedrooms and more than 10 bathrooms across 16,079 square feet of living space. At the current asking price, the home is valued at approximately $4,198 per square foot, the report shared. Its size, location and collection of private amenities place it firmly among the most expensive celebrity properties currently available in the Los Angeles area.Mediterranean style meets modern luxury The mansion makes a dramatic statement with its Mediterranean-inspired architecture, grand proportions and ornate details. Inside, formal living and entertaining rooms have high ceilings, large windows and multiple fireplaces. French doors and expansive windows help to connect the interiors with the landscaped grounds, creating a sense of openness despite the home’s highly traditional design. The kitchen is designed for both daily use and large-scale entertaining. It features high-end Wolf and Miele appliances, as well as a butler’s pantry that provides extra storage and preparation space. An informal dining area offers a more relaxed setting than the formal rooms, while nearby doors open towards a patio surrounded by fountains.One of the home’s more distinctive features is its wine cellar. Accessed by a staircase decorated with herringbone-patterned brickwork, the cellar adds another layer of old-world character to the estate. The property also includes colourful wallpaper, chandeliers and richly decorated lounging spaces, reinforcing its elaborate, classic style.The estate’s design extends well beyond the main residence. The compound has dedicated staff facilities and a guesthouse, providing staff and visitors their own space but with privacy within the main house. This is an ideal design for a property of this size, allowing entertainment and household activities to take place independently of the owners. The primary suite functions as a private sanctuary rather than just a bedroom. It features a sitting area, separate bathrooms and large wardrobe areas. The extra room allows the suite to be a self-contained part of the mansion, with room for both leisure and personal activities.Outside, the grounds have been extensively landscaped to create a secluded setting. A large swimming pool serves as the centrepiece of the outdoor entertainment area, while the property’s elevated position offers views of the surrounding city skyline and nearby mountains. The grounds are designed to feel more like a private resort than a conventional backyard.Sports and recreation are also central to the estate’s appeal. The property includes a clay tennis court accompanied by an entertainment pavilion, creating a dedicated space for both games and social gatherings. A four-car garage and large motor court provide ample room for vehicles, guests and arrivals.Together, the pool, tennis court, pavilion, guesthouse, staff quarters and landscaped grounds give the property an unusually comprehensive character. For the next owner, the mansion offers the privacy of a gated retreat while remaining close to the lifestyle and prestige associated with Beverly Hills.The current listing also comes at a time when the McGraws continue to hold a substantial property portfolio. Realtor.com reported that the couple owns several other California residences, including a Calabasas mansion purchased in 2011 for $6.6 million and another Beverly Hills property bought for $10 million in 2020. That home is understood to be used mainly by their son Jordan McGraw and his wife, Morgan Stewart.The couple also owns a mansion in Dallas, which Dr. Phil purchased in 2020 after it had been listed for just under $12 million. Their Beverly Hills estate, however, remains the most ambitious property in the portfolio now being offered to the market.At $67.5 million, the residence is aimed at a buyer seeking more than square footage. It offers a complete luxury lifestyle, with grand architecture, private guest facilities, resort-style outdoor spaces and a location associated with celebrity Los Angeles. Whether the property achieves its full asking price will depend on the market and the buyer’s appetite for a highly personalised estate, but the listing already highlights the remarkable rise in value of the home since the McGraws purchased it in 2010.
Article Summary: The 16,079-square-foot estate has been listed for $67.5 million. The asking price is more than double the couple’s original purchase cost. The couple purchased the property for $29.8 million in 2010. The estate includes eight bedrooms and more than 10 bathrooms.

Article Title: On a 160-acre Nebraska farm parcel, one wind turbine and its equipment use about 1 acre; the developer says a typical 30-year lease averages $10,000 to $12,500 a year, versus about $600 for top-dollar
Article Text:
The turbine sends electricity to a nearby power station, from where it is supplied to local customers.

How does the farmer earn money?

Why wind turbine was installed on farmland?

Rotor being installed on a wind turbine

2.5 megawatts of electricity produced

Benefits for the local community

A farmer in Nebraska, United States, is earning additional income by leasing part of his agricultural land for a wind turbine. A wind energy company has leased his 160-acre property to install a wind turbine, but the turbine and its equipment take up only about one acre. The farmer can continue using the remaining 159 acres for agriculture.The financial difference is significant. According to the National Rural Electric Cooperative Association (NRECA), the company behind the project says a typical 30-year lease pays an average of $10,000 to $12,500 a year. In comparison, even a highly productive acre of corn might bring in around $600 annually. The figures were shared in a case study published by NRECA in July 2021.The wind turbine is part of a project in Cuming County, Nebraska, where a local electricity provider wanted to produce some of its own power instead of buying all its electricity from larger suppliers. The company, Bluestem Energy Solutions, installed the turbine in 2019 and sells the electricity it produces to Cuming County Public Power District (CCPPD), which serves homes and businesses in the area.Matt Robinette, vice president of development at Bluestem Energy Solutions, explained that the company signs leases covering the entire piece of land, even though it needs only a small area for the turbine."The landowner is free to utilize the other 159 acres for whatever purposes they prefer," Robinette said.The agreement lasts for 30 years, with an option to extend it. According to the company, a typical lease pays an average of $10,000 to $12,500 annually over this period. The payments start at a lower amount and gradually increase each year.Chet McWhorter, general manager of CCPPD, explained why the arrangement is financially attractive for the farmer. "Even if it was top dollar corn and the landowner was the best farmer in the world, he might be getting $600 an acre, so he's doing very well with the lease," McWhorter said.However, the $10,000 to $12,500 figure represents the company's typical lease payments, not the confirmed annual income of this particular farmer.The idea began in 2016 when CCPPD was negotiating a new electricity supply agreement. The district wanted to produce some electricity locally to reduce its dependence on outside suppliers and keep costs more predictable.It first explored solar power and even installed solar panels on its office building to see how well they worked.However, the area frequently experiences cloudy and rainy weather, making a larger solar project less financially attractive. Adding batteries to store solar electricity would also have been too expensive at the time.The district then turned towards wind energy after one of its directors visited another wind turbine project in Nebraska.CCPPD initially considered owning a turbine itself, but the cost was too high. It eventually partnered with Bluestem Energy Solutions, which agreed to build, own and maintain the turbine.The project cost approximately $4.5 million, which Bluestem funded. CCPPD instead agreed to buy the electricity generated by the turbine for 30 years.The wind turbine installed in Cuming County is a General Electric model capable of producing up to 2.5 megawatts of electricity.It stands on an 89-metre tower and reaches approximately 152 metres when one of its blades points straight upwards.According to the NRECA case study, the turbine was expected to generate around 10,950 megawatt-hours of electricity each year. CCPPD estimated that this would be enough to supply electricity to more than 900 homes.The turbine sends electricity to a nearby power station, from where it is supplied to local customers. This means the district does not need to purchase the same amount of electricity from its larger supplier.The turbine recorded a capacity factor of 56.17% in 2020. In simple terms, this measures how much electricity it actually generated compared with what it could have produced if it had operated at full capacity throughout the year.The benefits extend beyond the farmer receiving lease payments. According to the 2021 case study, the turbine had helped CCPPD reduce its annual electricity costs by around 3% to 4%.The district also estimated that the project would contribute more than $1 million to the local economy over its 30-year life.It brings in approximately $11,000 in additional property taxes each year, with 60% of that money going to public schools.The project also supports local businesses when maintenance workers visit the area and spend money on hotels, fuel and food.Bluestem is responsible for maintaining the turbine, so CCPPD does not have to pay separately for repairs or regular servicing.Another advantage is that the electricity price is agreed upon in advance. While the cost of electricity purchased from other suppliers can change, the wind power agreement gives the district a clearer idea of what it will pay in the coming years. "The nice thing about wind is we know exactly what it's going to cost," McWhorter said.
Article Summary: Wind turbine is part of a project in Cuming County, Nebraska, where a local electricity provider wanted to produce some of its own power. The company behind the project says a typical 30-year lease pays an average of $10,000 to $12,500 a year. In comparison, even a highly productive acre of corn might bring in around $600 annually.

Article Title: Burmese python males undergo a dramatic seasonal hormone shift before breeding; scientists tracked testosterone and corticosterone in Florida snakes
Article Text:
Burmese python coiled in the grass in the Everglades. Image Credit: Wikipedia

How does testosterone change before Burmese python breeding

Burmese python. Image Credit: Wikipedia

What did the Florida snake study measure

Difference in the levels of corticosterone

What does the hormone cycle reveal about winter breeding

Burmese python males in South Florida undergo a marked seasonal change in testosterone as the breeding period approaches, while another hormone linked to stress and energy use follows a less predictable pattern. A study published in General and Comparative Endocrinology tracked testosterone and corticosterone in free-ranging male Burmese pythons to examine how their hormone levels change across the year. The researchers found that testosterone rises before breeding, and then falls steadily, while corticosterone varies more widely during the breeding period without showing the same clear seasonal cycle.The clearest shift involved testosterone, a hormone closely associated with male reproduction. According to the study, testosterone increased as the breeding period approached and reached its highest levels in November, just before breeding began. It then declined through the breeding season before returning to baseline levels during the non-breeding months.That timing is important because it suggests that the hormonal preparation for reproduction begins before the main breeding period itself. The researchers describe November as a distinct pre-breeding period, refining the way the reproductive cycle of male Burmese pythons can be understood.The study also found a strong relationship between testosterone and day length. As the days became shorter towards winter, testosterone increased. Day length was negatively associated with testosterone in the researchers' best-supported seasonal model, making the changing amount of daylight one of the strongest environmental clues linked to the hormone cycle.The researchers followed free-ranging adult male Burmese pythons in South Florida rather than relying only on captive animals. They collected samples throughout the year from September 2019 to October 2024, gathering 110 samples from 79 individual snakes. Most of the sampling took place in Big Cypress National Preserve, with additional snakes coming from public and private lands in south-west Florida.The researchers measured two hormones, testosterone and corticosterone. They also considered factors that could help explain changes in hormone levels, including body condition, month, average daily temperature, day length and the time between capture and blood collection. This allowed the study to separate broader seasonal patterns from short-term effects associated with capturing the snakes.The work was designed to address a gap in knowledge about the reproductive biology of an invasive population. Although Burmese pythons have been established in South Florida for more than two decades, the researchers noted that their reproductive physiology remains incompletely understood.Corticosterone did not follow the same neat seasonal pattern as testosterone. The study found no clear annual trend in corticosterone, although levels varied more during the breeding season. Post-hoc comparisons showed that corticosterone was higher during breeding months from November through March, while its lowest levels were recorded in September. Its numerical peak occurred in July, meaning its pattern did not simply rise and fall alongside reproduction.Temperature provided another important clue. The researchers found a negative relationship between average temperature and corticosterone, meaning corticosterone tended to be higher when temperatures were lower. The best-supported model during the reproductive season included body condition, average temperature and the time taken to collect blood.The time taken to collect blood mattered because capture itself can affect corticosterone. By including this factor in their analysis, the researchers could better distinguish the immediate response to capture from the snakes' underlying hormone levels.The combined results point to a distinctive reproductive rhythm in South Florida. The researchers established that Burmese pythons are winter breeders, with reproductive preparation building as daylight decreases and temperatures fall. Testosterone reaches its peak in November, followed by breeding from early December into mid-March.The study also connects this timing with the environmental conditions of South Florida. The researchers suggest that the snakes may be responding to seasonal cues resembling those associated with the dry season in their native range. In South Florida, breeding begins around November, while egg laying begins in May and hatchlings emerge from July to October.For male pythons, this seasonal preparation is also linked to reproductive behaviour. During the breeding period, males increase their movements while searching for females and can form breeding groups. The hormone results provide a clearer physiological picture of the period when these behaviours occur.The study notes that current removal methods can be labour-intensive and expensive, while some approaches rely on males locating reproductive females. Understanding physiological signs associated with mate-searching could contribute to more targeted management methods.The researchers also stress that the hormone picture is not complete. They point to other parts of the reproductive system that have not yet been fully examined, including hormones involved in regulating the reproductive pathway and metabolic hormones.
Article Summary: Researchers tracked testosterone and corticosterone in free-ranging male Burmese pythons to examine how their hormone levels change across the year. The clearest shift involved testosterone, a hormone closely associated with male reproduction. Testosterone reaches its peak in November, followed by breeding from early December into mid-March.

Article Title: Birmingham council sold a £395,000 house in 2013; 11 years later, it discovered a primary school had accidentally gone with it; now it is going to court to get it back
Article Text:
George Dixon Primary School, Image: Pentagon Play

A Birmingham house sale that came with a school

The buyer was a company, not Bains personally

The case in the High Court

The school stays open

Birmingham City Council sold a three-bedroom former caretaker's house at auction in 2013 for £395,000, and a paperwork error meant the sale also transferred ownership of George Dixon Primary School in Edgbaston. The mistake went unnoticed for 11 years while the school carried on as normal. It came to light on 12 April 2024, when the school looked into becoming an academy and learned that the council no longer owned the site. The council has since launched High Court proceedings in London against NH Care Ltd, the care provider that bought the house, and Lloyds Bank, its lender.The house, on Fountain Road, was originally built for the school's caretaker, and its back garden borders the school's playing fields. It was bought at auction by NH Care Ltd, a company linked to businessman Sukhjit Bains, 50. Both the house and the school were registered under the same Land Registry title, which became the root of the problem when the sale paperwork was drawn up.The transfer was drafted on a TR1, the form used to transfer an entire registered title, rather than a TP1, which transfers only part of one. Because the house and school shared a title, the TR1 handed over both.According to the council, the form was prepared on behalf of the buyer, yet the council's own conveyancer signed it off without spotting the error.Although Bains is the businessman most often named in coverage, the purchaser was NH Care Ltd. Bains and the company's two other directors are reported to have been unaware that the school had been included until the council contacted them. NH Care has reportedly not yet filed a response to the claim.After spotting the error, the council approached the company to resolve the matter. The council says Bains initially agreed to return the school, but that communication then stopped and the necessary paperwork was never signed. With no resolution, it turned to the courts.The council is asking the court to correct the register and restore its ownership of the school. By its account, the original contract covered only the house, so the transfer document did not reflect what was agreed. It also argues the mistake was mutual, since the incorrect form was drafted by the buyer's lawyers and executed by the council's conveyancer. Finally, it says that selling school land and playing fields requires the consent of the Secretary of State, which was never obtained. A council spokesman said it is "pursuing the appropriate legal process to rectify the position."George Dixon Primary School, which has around 324 pupils, has continued to operate throughout. The house, meanwhile, has reportedly stood empty since the sale.The case lands as the council, which effectively declared itself bankrupt in September 2023, works through a large programme of property disposals. A sale that was meant to dispose of a former caretaker's house instead produced a dispute over a primary school, and a High Court claim to unwind it more than a decade later.
Article Summary: Birmingham City Council sold a three-bedroom former caretaker's house at auction in 2013 for £395,000. A paperwork error meant the sale also transferred ownership of George Dixon Primary School. The mistake went unnoticed for 11 years while the school carried on as normal. It came to light on 12 April 2024, when the school looked into becoming an academy and learned that the council no longer owned the site.

Article Title: ‘Angry and confused’: Tennessee death row inmate Christa Pike wakes up after surviving execution attempt
Article Text:
A picture taken on December 4, 2007 shows death row inmate Christa Pike entering a Knox County Criminal Court in Knoxville, Tennessee, US

Judge orders evidence from execution preserved

Could Tennessee try to execute Pike again?

US death-row inmate Christa Pike woke up “angry and confused” in a Tennessee hospital days after surviving a botched lethal injection, her lawyer said on Wednesday.Pike’s first words after regaining consciousness were “Where am I?” and “Who are you?”on Tuesday in what her lawyer described as a “shock to everyone”. Her legal team had believed for days that she was brain dead and expected doctors to withdraw life support.Pike is believed to be the only person to survive an execution attempt by lethal injection.She remembers only limited details of the September 30 execution attempt, during which she was administered two rounds of the drug pentobarbital.“We don't know the toll all of this will take” on her mental health, Spivey said, describing her as “angry and confused” after the ordeal.A Tennessee judge on Wednesday ordered the state to preserve all evidence connected to the failed execution after Pike’s lawyers sought an emergency order.The order covers items from the execution room, including IV lines and syringes, as well as packaging, inserts and labels. The judge also ordered the preservation of documentation concerning Pike’s psychological condition before, during and after the execution.Pike’s lawyer Luke Ihnen told the court that communication with his client had been difficult because she had remained unconscious until Tuesday and was now only “speaking limitedly”.The legal team said the preserved evidence could form the basis of a future lawsuit against the state.Tennessee could attempt to execute Pike again, but any effort to use lethal injection is likely to face significant legal challenges, according to Tennessee-based defence attorney Stephen Ross Johnson, BBC reported.“For the state to attempt to execute her again using the same methodology, they would have severe legal hurdles,” Johnson said.Johnson said Pike’s medical condition, combined with the failed execution, could make it difficult for the state to justify another attempt using lethal injection.Tennessee could also seek to execute Pike using a different method, although that would involve additional legal hurdles and potentially require approval from the governor’s office and state legislature.
Article Summary: Pike's first words after regaining consciousness were “Where am I?” and “Who are you?’ Her legal team had believed for days that she was brain dead and expected doctors to withdraw life support. A Tennessee judge on Wednesday ordered the state to preserve all evidence connected to the failed execution.

Article Title: 'No excuse for victim blaming': Mamdani under fire from Democrats and pro-Palestinian left over Oct 7 message
Article Text:
File photo: New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani attends a vigil marking the third anniversary of the October 7 attacks on Israel Wednesday, Oct. 7, 2026, in New York. (AP Photo/Frank Franklin II)

Pro-Palestinian left's critique of Mamdani

New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani ’s statement marking the third anniversary of Hamas’ October 7 attack on Israel has drawn criticism from both sides of the US political divide. Democrats and Jewish groups accusing him of shifting attention from the victims of the attack to Israel’s war in Gaza, while some on the pro-Palestinian left say he did not go far enough.Mamdani’s statement began by calling October 7, 2023, a “profoundly painful” day and condemning Hamas’ “horrific war crimes”, including the killing of about 1,200 people in Israel and the taking of more than 250 hostages.“We grieve alongside our many friends and neighbors who still carry that unthinkable loss,” he said.But Mamdani then turned to Israel’s military campaign in Gaza, calling it a “devastating, ongoing genocide” and citing more than 74,000 deaths recorded by the Hamas-controlled Gaza health ministry.“Many New Yorkers are reckoning with this unbearable grief, and we mourn alongside them — all while knowing that our tax dollars fund these war crimes,” Mamdani said.He added that three years later, “occupation and apartheid continue”, while accusing the US federal government of complicity through arms shipments.The statement drew fierce criticism from several Democratic lawmakers, who said Mamdani had made the anniversary about Israel rather than Hamas and the people killed and abducted on October 7.Florida representative Debbie Wasserman Schultz accused Mamdani of “desecrating the memory of murdered, innocent Jews”, while New Jersey representative Josh Gottheimer said the mayor was “blaming the victims”. Jersey City mayor Steven Fulop called the statement “inappropriate and unnecessarily inflammatory”.New York representative Dan Goldman called the message “egregious and insulting”. Goldman told Politico that October 7 should be reserved for remembering what he described as a horrific terror attack, rather than using the occasion to focus on the broader conflict.“Regardless of what you actually think of the conflict and what’s happened either since or before, there’s no excuse for victim blaming,” Goldman said.Brad Lander, the Mamdani-backed Democrat who defeated Goldman in this year’s primary, took a more nuanced position. He condemned Hamas but argued against forcing people to choose between mourning the victims of October 7 and acknowledging Palestinian suffering.“We can mourn for those lost on October 7th and still acknowledge the enormous imbalance of power between Israel and the Palestinians,” Lander wrote.Mamdani also faced criticism from Jewish organisations. Anti-Defamation League CEO Jonathan Greenblatt said the mayor’s statement did not mention Jews and accused him of using a day meant for mourning the victims of the attack to repeat his anti-Zionist arguments.US ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee called the statement an “outrageous & disgusting rant”, while Ofir Akunis, Israel’s consul general in New York, called it a “disgrace, shame, and insult to the memory of those who were murdered”.But the backlash did not come only from critics of Mamdani’s position on Israel.Some on the pro-Palestinian left also attacked the mayor, arguing that his stance did not go far enough. About 200 anti-Israel protesters gathered outside City Hall on Wednesday evening, with some accusing Mamdani of betraying the Palestinian cause.Several protesters told Politico they had voted for Mamdani but would not support him for re-election because they were unhappy that he had not fired NYPD commissioner Jessica Tisch, whom they described as a Zionist, or stopped some New York synagogues from hosting events promoting land sales in the occupied West Bank.The protesters’ criticism reflected a broader frustration among some activists that Mamdani, despite his longstanding opposition to Israel’s policies, had not gone far enough in confronting Israel or supporting the Palestinian cause.At the same time, senator Bernie Sanders, an independent who is a close adviser to Mamdani, defended the mayor’s basic framing of the conflict. Sanders said Israel had the right to defend itself and target Hamas after the October 7 attack, but accused Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government of waging “a genocide against the Palestinian people in Gaza”.Mamdani’s statement had drawn more than 11 million views on X by Wednesday eveningThe controversy reflects the difficult political position Mamdani has occupied throughout his rise to power. His strong criticism of Israel helped energise young and progressive voters during his mayoral campaign, while also making him a frequent target of Jewish groups, Israeli officials and more moderate Democrats.Mamdani has consistently rejected accusations of antisemitism, arguing that criticism of Israel and its government is distinct from hostility towards Jewish people.
Article Summary: New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani's statement marking the third anniversary of Hamas’ October 7 attack on Israel has drawn criticism from both sides of the US political divide. Democrats and Jewish groups accuse him of shifting attention from the victims of the attack to Israel’s war in Gaza. Some on the pro- Palestinian left say he did not go far enough.

Article Title: Syria considers sending troops to Saudi Arabia to fight Houthis
Article Text:
Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa meets Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia (Reuters)

Syria-Saudi relations

The bigger picture

Syria is considering sending troops to Saudi Arabia to help fight Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen, Reuters reported, citing a US official and a Syrian military official familiar with the discussions.According to Reuters, Syria is looking at several options, from providing defensive support and expertise to help Saudi Arabia counter Houthi missile and drone attacks, to potentially sending Syrian troops to fight alongside Saudi-backed Yemeni forces.No final decision has been taken, and Damascus has not confirmed any plan to deploy combat troops.The US official told Reuters that Saudi Arabia had asked Syria to deploy forces to fight the Houthis. However, the Syrian government has not publicly confirmed that it has agreed to send troops to Yemen.A Syrian diplomat told Reuters that Damascus “stood firmly with Saudi Arabia” against Houthi attacks but stressed that Syria's priority remained its domestic recovery after years of war. The diplomat said any military cooperation or exchange of expertise with Saudi Arabia would take place “exclusively through official channels” and under existing bilateral agreements.The development comes as Saudi Arabia steps up its military campaign against the Houthis after the Iran-backed group intensified attacks on Saudi territory.The possible Syrian military support for Saudi Arabia comes as relations between Damascus and Riyadh have strengthened significantly since Ahmed al-Sharaa took power.Saudi Arabia has emerged as an important political and economic partner for Syria as the new government tries to rebuild the country after 14 years of civil war.In February, Syria and Saudi Arabia signed a multibillion-dollar investment package covering aviation, energy, real estate and telecommunications, underscoring Riyadh's role in Syria's economic recovery.Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa met Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman in Riyadh on October 6. According to Syria's state news agency SANA, the two leaders discussed bilateral relations, regional developments and ways to expand cooperation between the two countries.Since the fall of Bashar al-Assad, Damascus has largely tried to avoid getting pulled into regional wars while concentrating on rebuilding its institutions and integrating former rebel groups into a new Syrian army.Reuters reported that Syria had previously rejected a US request to help fight Hezbollah in Lebanon for similar reasons.A decision to help Saudi Arabia against the Houthis would therefore represent a major shift. The Houthis are backed by Iran, while Saudi Arabia is now leading a renewed campaign against the group after weeks of missile and drone attacks on the kingdom.For Saudi Arabia, bringing Syria into the conflict could provide another Arab partner as Saudi-backed Yemeni forces attempt to push back the Houthis.For al-Sharaa, however, sending Syrian troops could expose his still-fragile military to a new conflict and risk worsening relations with Iran, Hezbollah and Iran-aligned Iraqi militias.
Article Summary: Syria is considering sending troops to Saudi Arabia to help fight Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen. No final decision has been taken, and Damascus has not confirmed any plan to deploy combat troops. Saudi Arabia is leading a renewed campaign against the Houthis after weeks of missile and drone attacks on the kingdom.

Article Title: 'Not bragging, just telling facts': Trump makes fresh pitch for Nobel Peace Prize, citing 'eight settled wars'
Article Text:
This is not the first time Trump has said he deserves the Nobel Peace Prize.

US President Donald Trump on Wednesday said he deserves the Nobel Peace Prize, while acknowledging that he remains unsure whether the Norwegian Nobel Committee will select him for the 2026 award.Speaking to reporters in the Oval Office, Trump said the announcement was imminent and suggested that the committee may not favour him.“I don't know what their decision is going to be,” Trump said of the 2026 award, which the Norwegian Nobel Committee will announce on Friday. “They have a ​reputation for maybe not giving it to people like me,” he added.“It is about that time,” Trump remarked. “But I was very honoured to receive it indirectly last time by the recipient, who said nobody in history deserves it more than President Trump.”This is not the first time Trump has said he deserves the Nobel Peace Prize. Trump has repeatedly claimed that his diplomatic interventions since returning to the White House have helped resolve multiple international conflicts.“I’ve done stuff that nobody else has ever done. I’m not bragging, I’m just telling you the facts. No president has probably ever settled any wars. I settled eight wars.”“But, whether I get it or not, I have done far more. And I think it would be a great discredit to them.And I’m not saying that out of scorn, I’m saying that when you settle eight wars, and nobody’s never,” he added.Trump has also credited his administration’s trade and economic pressure, including threatened tariffs, with pushing countries towards diplomatic engagement. However, his claims about the extent of those diplomatic achievements have faced challenges, with conflicts continuing or resurfacing in several regions.Trump also criticised former US President Barack Obama, who received the Nobel Peace Prize in 2009. “Obama got it, and he didn’t do anything,” Trump stated. “He still doesn’t know what he got it for. He got it when he got elected, right at the beginning, and he had no idea why he got it.”Trump also referred to Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado, who won last year’s Nobel Peace Prize.“Last time they gave it to a young lady who’s a fabulous person, and she said she didn’t deserve it, that I deserved it, and she gave it to me,” Trump said.Machado has previously praised Trump and said she wanted to share the honour with him. However, the Norwegian Nobel Institute has clarified that the Nobel Peace Prize itself cannot be transferred or shared.“A Nobel Prize cannot be revoked nor transferred to others. Once the laureate or laureates are announced, the decision is final,” said Erik Aasheim, a spokesperson for the Norwegian Nobel Institute.Aasheim added that while the prize itself cannot be transferred, laureates are free to dispose of the prize money as they wish.The 2026 Nobel Peace Prize winner will be announced on October 9, with the award ceremony scheduled for December 10. The prize is decided independently by the Norwegian Nobel Committee in Oslo.
Article Summary: The 2026 Nobel Peace Prize winner will be announced on October 9, with the award ceremony scheduled for December 10. The prize is decided independently by the Norwegian Nobel Committee in Oslo. Trump has repeatedly claimed that his diplomatic interventions since returning to the White House have helped resolve multiple international conflicts.

Article Title: A 2,600-acre South Carolina timber property at the rivers where Revolutionary War commander Francis Marion hid from British forces has been transferred to the state, advancing a 7,600-acre conservatio
Article Text:
During the American Revolutionary War, Marion and his militia used the area's remote swamps as a base for military operations

Francis Marion and the swamps

7,600-acre wildlife habitat

Flood protection from forest

Funding the conservation

A 2,600-acre timber property in South Carolina, located near the rivers where Revolutionary War commander Francis Marion once hid from British forces, has been transferred to the state's Department of Natural Resources. The land, known as River Forks, forms part of a larger 7,600-acre conservation project that aims to protect wildlife habitats, historic sites and areas that help reduce flooding.The Open Space Institute (OSI), a non-profit conservation organisation, transferred the property to the South Carolina Department of Natural Resources (SCDNR). According to Vise Voter, the transfer, announced on Tuesday includes 11 miles of riverfront and marks the first phase of the Snow's Island Assemblage conservation project.The wider project covers two properties in Florence County including the 5,000-acre Snow's Island and the adjoining 2,600-acre River Forks timber tract. Together, they include more than 60 miles of riverfront along the Lynches and Great Pee Dee Rivers. OSI acquired both properties in 2024.Snow's Island is located where the Lynches and Great Pee Dee Rivers meet. During the American Revolutionary War, Marion and his militia used the area's remote swamps as a base for military operations against British troops.The surrounding waterways and wetlands provided a place from which Marion could organise raids. According to OSI, his militia launched several attacks from the area, including a major assault on the British garrison at Georgetown, located downstream along the Pee Dee River.The conservation project is intended to protect this historic landscape while eventually allowing people to visit the area. Once the land becomes part of the state's Heritage Preserve and Wildlife Management Area programmes, visitors will have opportunities to explore the swamps associated with Marion's wartime activities.The property, however, remains closed to the public while SCDNR works towards completing the larger conservation project.The Snow's Island Assemblage contains several types of natural habitats, including bottomland hardwood forests, upland pine forests and floodplains. These areas support wildlife and connect with other protected lands in the region.The 2,600-acre River Forks property alone provides habitat for 140 high-priority conservation species, including 15 species listed as at risk under federal or state classifications.Among the wildlife associated with the wider conservation area are the Swallow-tailed Kite and Spotted Turtle. Protecting such a large stretch of connected land is intended to help animals move between habitats without the barriers created when natural areas are divided into smaller parcels.The project also strengthens an existing network of protected land that includes the 25,000-acre Woodbury Wildlife Management Area.Flood protection is another major reason behind the conservation effort. The property contains extensive forested wetlands and floodplains that can hold large quantities of water during heavy rainfall.These floodplains work like natural sponges, absorbing water when rivers rise and releasing it gradually. This helps reduce the amount of floodwater moving downstream at once.The importance of these natural floodplains became clear during Hurricane Florence in 2018, when severe flooding affected parts of South Carolina.Flood data published in the Journal of South Carolina Water Resources showed that the large floodplain between the Pee Dee, Lynches and Little Pee Dee Rivers stored more than one million acre-feet of water during the hurricane. That water was released gradually over ten days, helping protect communities downstream.The Snow's Island Assemblage lies within this floodplain, making its protection important for the region's long-term flood management.The project involves cooperation between conservation organisations, state agencies, local authorities and private foundations.Funding for the River Forks acquisition included $3 million from the US Fish and Wildlife Service. The wider conservation effort also received support from the South Carolina Office of Resilience, South Carolina Conservation Bank, Darla Moore Foundation and Knobloch Family Foundation.Florence County Council voted in July 2024 to contribute $1.5 million from its capital sales tax fund towards acquiring the Snow's Island Assemblage. According to OSI, this was the county's first investment in land conservation.The properties were previously owned by Manulife Investment Management and Weyerhaeuser before OSI acquired them in 2024.The transfer of River Forks is the first stage of bringing the entire Snow's Island Assemblage under state management. The remaining land is expected to be transferred to SCDNR in early 2027. Once the process is completed, the state plans to manage the protected landscape through its Wildlife Management Area and Heritage Trust programmes.
Article Summary: The land, known as River Forks, forms part of a larger 7,600-acre conservation project that aims to protect wildlife habitats, historic sites and areas that help reduce flooding. During the American Revolutionary War, Francis Marion and his militia used the area's remote swamps as a base for military operations.

Article Title: East Hampton wants to spend $36.3 million to buy 38.3 acres of a former New York sand mine once slated for a 50-lot commercial subdivision; 33.3 acres would instead become open space
Article Text:
A major change from earlier development plans

What the $36.3 million would cover

A property with environmental significance

East Hampton Town is moving toward a multimillion-dollar purchase that could dramatically change the future of a large former sand mine in Wainscott, New York. The East Hampton Star first reported the proposed $36.3 million acquisition on October 1, while Long Island Life & Politics reported this week that the town sees the purchase as a way to preserve the property while retaining part of it for future municipal needs. The town is seeking to acquire 38.3 acres of the 70.5-acre property at 104 Wainscott Northwest Road. Under the proposal, about 33.3 acres would be designated for parks, recreation and open space, while roughly five acres would be reserved for municipal purposes. The town has not yet determined a specific use for that smaller portion. The property sits in the middle of Wainscott’s commercial area, north of Montauk Highway and near the headwaters of Georgica Pond. Its location has made the site a particularly significant piece of undeveloped land in a densely watched part of East Hampton.The proposed acquisition would mark a sharp departure from plans that have occupied East Hampton’s planning boards for years. The property was the subject of the Wainscott Commercial Center proposal, which sought to divide roughly 70 acres of the former sand and gravel mine into 50 commercial-industrial lots.East Hampton’s own planning documents describe the site as a reclaimed 70.51-acre sand and gravel mine in a Commercial-Industrial zoning district.The development proposal became one of the most contentious projects to come before the town. A public hearing in 2023 lasted eight hours and was split into two sessions, according to The East Hampton Star. Earlier discussions also highlighted the unusual environmental characteristics of the property. The former mine has very shallow groundwater in places, with an earlier town discussion noting depths of as little as 2.3 feet. Officials and residents had considered how redevelopment could affect groundwater, drainage and the broader watershed around Georgica Pond.The proposed purchase would be the second-largest amount East Hampton Town has spent on a single parcel, according to The East Hampton Star. The town paid $56 million for a 30-acre property on Wainscott’s Main Street in late 2024. The financing would be split between two sources. About 86.95% of the purchase would come from Community Preservation Fund money for the open-space portion, while 13.05% would be financed through bonds for the five-acre municipal section.The town is also expected to amend its management and stewardship plan for Community Preservation Fund properties as part of the transaction. A public hearing on the proposed acquisition is scheduled for October 15 at 6 p.m., giving residents an opportunity to weigh in before the purchase moves forward.The site’s environmental importance has been part of the debate long before the current acquisition proposal. A 2022 environmental impact statement prepared for the commercial-center application described the property as a reclaimed former sand and gravel mine and examined the consequences of turning it into a large commercial subdivision.The Wainscott hamlet planning process had previously considered a range of alternatives for the property, including open space, recreation, shared parking, affordable housing, renewable energy and transportation improvements. The latest proposal would preserve most of the 38.3 acres rather than divide that portion into commercial lots. For now, the five-acre municipal section remains the biggest question mark. The town would retain flexibility over its eventual use while placing the overwhelming majority of the acquired land under open-space and recreation purposes.If approved, the deal would transform a property that spent years at the center of a commercial development battle into one that is largely intended to remain open, giving East Hampton control over one of Wainscott’s largest remaining tracts while leaving a smaller area available for future public needs.
Article Summary: The town is seeking to acquire 38.3 acres of the 70.5-acre property at 104 Wainscott Northwest Road. The property sits in the middle of the commercial area, north of Montauk Highway and near the headwaters of Georgica Pond. A public hearing on the proposed acquisition is scheduled for October 15 at 6 p.m.

Article Title: After more than six generations of family ownership, a Massachusetts nonprofit raised over $4.9 million to buy 5.23-acre Holly Hill Farm and permanently protect the centuries-old piece of farmland
Article Text:
Beyond the vegetable rows

Poll Vote & Share your view What do you think is the biggest benefit of preserving community farms? Protecting farmland Supporting local communities Promoting sustainable farming Providing educational opportunities 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

For generations, Holly Hill Farm belonged to the same family. Now, after more than six generations of White family ownership, the 5.23-acre Massachusetts property has been secured for the future as a working farm, thanks to a fundraising effort by Friends of Holly Hill Farm (FHHF), according to a report by Cohasset Anchor. The nonprofit raised more than $4.9 million to buy the land and invest in its buildings and infrastructure, including $1 million in community preservation funds from the Town of Cohasset. This September 2026 purchase means the farm will remain a working farm and community resource permanently.FHHF will own and operate the farm, and a Conservation Restriction (CR) has also been placed on the part of the land that was not previously protected. The restriction, jointly held by Wildlands Trust and the Town of Cohasset, will permanently prevent future development on the land.“This is a once-in-a-generation accomplishment for the community, and a huge win for the environment and this beautiful farm. We are incredibly grateful to the White family and the community of Keep Our Farm a Farm supporters who made it possible to protect this precious land. However, our farm is more than the land, and we’re asking the community to join us to help ensure we can grow, teach, and be here for the community for generations to come,” Meredith Laban, Executive Director of Friends of Holly Hill Farm, said in a statement.Jean White, the co-founder of the farm, said this moment is a fulfilment of her husband Frank’s wishes. “Our family is enormously grateful for the efforts expended by all those in the community who worked on this initiative and the many extraordinary friends who helped make this happen. This teaching farm is a community resource for all ages, and will be preserved in perpetuity.”Though the land is protected, the nonprofit will continue to raise funds for its next phase, including making improvements to the historic 1785 barn, which houses the year-round farm stand. Better traffic flow and parking, as well as a heated, year-round indoor classroom with a working kitchen for teaching and preparing food for pantries, plus restrooms, are also part of the upcoming phase.Mark DeGiacomo, Board Chairperson of FHHM, remembered the efforts of its pioneers. “We want to honour our nonprofit’s co-founders, Jean and Frank White, and their family for their generosity, vision, and unwavering commitment to sustainable farming, education, community, and the land. Their passion and dedication laid the groundwork for Friends of Holly Hill Farm, shaped its mission, impacted the lives of countless people, and helped make the farm the community treasure it is to so many. We remain committed to keeping our farm a farm, to growing its future, and working with the community to ensure we can be here for many years to come.”Holly Hill is a certified organic farm growing vegetables, herbs, seedlings and flowers. The harvest travels further than the farm stand. Through its Farm to Food Pantry programme, food and flowers go to nine local food pantries. The stand supplies participating families through the Holly Hill Farm SHARES programme and accepts SNAP. There are also educational programmes. More than 20,000 students from over 14 communities take part in programmes on the farm, in classrooms and in school gardens each year, and partnerships reach more than 40 schools between the South Shore and Boston. The summer programmes have been named Best of the South Shore four years running.Adults also get workshops and guided walks led by the farm’s educators and outside experts. Tiered pricing and scholarships are offered so cost does not keep anyone out. It is a community deeply passionate about the land and its natural resources.
Article Summary: Friends of Holly Hill Farm raised more than $4.9 million to buy the land and invest in its buildings and infrastructure. This September 2026 purchase means the farm will remain a working farm and community resource permanently. A Conservation Restriction has also been placed on the part of the land that was not previously protected.

Article Title: An American elm has stood for more than 150 years and witnessed 33 US presidents despite the disease that wiped out millions of these trees
Article Text:
The Smithsonian Witness Elm, thought to be roughly 170 years old, bursts into greenery each spring. Image Credit: Smithsonian Gardens

How the historic American elm witnessed 33 US presidents

Importance of American elms to Washington

Young elms line the National Mall in this photo from 1942. Image Credit: Cornell University Library/Smithsonian Magazine

The Dutch elm disease changed that landscape

How the old tree continues to survive

What the Witness Elm reveals about long-term tree care

A historic American elm on the grounds of the Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History in Washington, D.C., has survived for more than 150 years, quietly witnessing generations of American history. Planted around 1850, the Smithsonian Witness Elm was already established decades before the museum opened in 1910. Since then, it has seen 33 US presidents, major national events and sweeping changes to the city around it. Its survival is especially remarkable because Dutch elm disease later killed millions of American elms across the country, leaving this tree as a living reminder of a once-common part of the American landscape.The Smithsonian Witness Elm stands near the corner of Constitution Avenue and Ninth Street, in the grounds of the National Museum of Natural History. According to the Smithsonian Magazine the tree is estimated to be more than 150 years old and has existed through the administrations of 33 presidents.The tree predates the museum beside it by roughly 60 years. When it was planted around 1850, Washington, D.C., looked very different. The surrounding landscape would gradually change as the National Mall developed and the city expanded, while the elm continued to grow in place.The Smithsonian Gardens Witness Tree information sheet , identifies it as an American elm, or Ulmus americana, and describes it as one of the oldest and most majestic trees on the Smithsonian grounds. Its position also gave it a remarkable view of events taking place between the White House and the US Capitol.American elms once played a major role in American cities. The Smithsonian Gardens document explains that the species is native to eastern North America and was widely planted throughout the United States during the 1700s and 1800s.Washington was particularly associated with the trees. According to Smithsonian Magazine, American elms became a defining part of the city's landscape, including the National Mall. Their graceful shape, shade and ability to tolerate urban conditions made them a popular choice.The Smithsonian Gardens document notes that elm trees were part of the earliest plans for the National Mall, where they helped connect parks, avenues and monument grounds. The resulting landscape created the broad avenue of trees that became such a familiar feature of central Washington.The survival of the Witness Elm becomes more remarkable when set against the history of Dutch elm disease. The Smithsonian Gardens document states that the fungus was introduced to the United States around 1930 and went on to kill millions of American elms throughout the country.Smithsonian Magazine provides more detail on the disease's impact. Dutch elm disease was first identified in the Netherlands in 1919 and detected in the United States in 1930. It is caused by a fungus that is commonly spread by European elm bark beetles. Once inside a tree, the fungus blocks the tissues that carry water and nutrients, causing leaves and branches to die.The disease reached Washington, D.C., in 1947. By the 1970s, the US Forest Service estimated that tens of millions of American elms had been killed. The loss was especially significant because cities had planted so many elms.The Smithsonian Witness Elm is not believed to possess the strong resistance to Dutch elm disease found in some other American elms. Smithsonian arborist Jake Hendee explained to Smithsonian Magazine that many large, old elms that remain today may simply have survived through a combination of chance and careful management.That management is extensive. The tree is about 85 feet tall and more than five feet in diameter, according to the Smithsonian Magazine. Its size means that staff must pay attention not only to disease but also to the physical weight and structure of its branches.Large metal cables are used on some trees to provide support, while structural pruning can reduce the weight placed on vulnerable parts. Specialists also use sonic tomography to look inside the tree and identify weak areas without drilling into its wood.The Witness Elm also receives preventative treatment. Smithsonian Magazine reports that the tree is injected with fungicide every three years to help protect it from Dutch elm disease.The Smithsonian Gardens document says the elm is carefully maintained by staff and was the first tree catalogued in the Smithsonian Gardens Tree Collection, a living collection containing thousands of trees.Its physical scale helps explain why it has attracted attention. The Smithsonian Gardens information sheet records a trunk circumference of 17.75 feet, a crown spread of 116.5 feet and a height of 80 feet. The Smithsonian Magazine article gives a later measurement of about 85 feet in height, showing the tree's continuing growth and the variation that can occur between measurements.Smithsonian arborists emphasise that relying heavily on one species can leave an entire landscape exposed to disease. A mixture of species and varieties gives city forests a better chance of withstanding possible threats.Today, its branches form a living link between the Washington of the nineteenth century and the city of the present.
Article Summary: The Smithsonian Witness Elm was planted in Washington, D.C., in 1850. It has witnessed 33 US presidents, major national events and sweeping changes to the city around it. Its survival is especially remarkable because Dutch elm disease later killed millions of American elms across the country.

Article Title: Ousted Venezuela's Maduro, wife likely to face fresh US charges over 'torture' of Americans
Article Text:
Supporters of Venezuela's government rally to demand the release of ousted President Nicolas Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores.

Maduro, Flores held in Brooklyn as trial approaches

The US could bring new criminal charges against ousted Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores as early as Thursday over allegations that Americans detained in Venezuela were tortured, a US official familiar with the investigation said on Wednesday.Maduro and Flores were captured by the US military from their home in Caracas on January 3 and brought to New York, where they are facing existing drug-trafficking charges. Both have pleaded not guilty and are scheduled to stand trial from June 1, 2027.Details of the potential new charges, including the identities of the alleged victims, were not immediately available.Washington has previously accused Maduro’s government of detaining Americans as leverage to seek concessions, including relief from US financial sanctions. Among those classified by the US as wrongfully detained were five oil executives arrested on graft charges who were released in 2022 as part of a prisoner swap.Two former US Army Special Forces members detained in Venezuela in 2020 following a failed operation aimed at ousting Maduro were also released in a 2023 prisoner exchange.Maduro, 63, and Flores, 69, are currently being held at a federal jail in Brooklyn. Since Maduro’s capture, Venezuela has been led by his former vice president Delcy Rodriguez, whose government has increased cooperation with the Trump administration.Flores is due to appear in Manhattan federal court on Thursday, where she is expected to seek release from custody before trial on health grounds. Prosecutors are opposing her request.
Article Summary: Maduro and Flores were captured by the US military from their home in Caracas on January 3 and brought to New York. They are facing existing drug-trafficking charges. Both have pleaded not guilty and are scheduled to stand trial from June 1, 2027.

Article Title: 'Expecting life-threatening impacts': Tropical storm Isaias to strike US Gulf Coast as hurricane
Article Text:
Isaias set to strengthen into a hurricane before hitting the US Gulf Coast

Tropical Storm Isaias formed Wednesday (local time) off eastern Mexico and was forecast to rapidly strengthen into the Atlantic season’s first hurricane before reaching the US Gulf Coast later this week, with landfall possible as early as Friday evening.The storm was packing maximum sustained winds of 65 mph and was moving east-northeast at 8 mph, the National Hurricane Center said. Forecasters expected Isaias to become a hurricane by Thursday as it turns north towards the Gulf Coast, with landfall likely late Friday or early Saturday.“We’re expecting multiple dangerous, life-threatening impacts along portions of the northern Gulf Coast beginning Friday and continuing into the weekend," National Hurricane Center director Michael Brennan said in a video briefing as quoted by news agency AP.Isaias could strengthen into a Category 3 hurricane, with winds of at least 111 mph, Brennan said. A hurricane watch was issued for the northern Gulf Coast from Bay St. Louis, Mississippi, to Indian Pass on Florida’s Panhandle.The storm could bring dangerous storm surge from southeast Louisiana to Florida’s Big Bend, while 3 to 7 inches of rain could trigger flash flooding along the coast. Rainfall of 1 to 3 inches was possible as far inland as Tennessee and the western Carolinas.Authorities moved to prepare for the storm, with Florida and Alabama declaring states of emergency. Gulf oil producers halted about 25% of regional oil production, taking roughly 511,000 barrels a day off the market.In Alabama, Gulf Shores canceled its National Shrimp Festival, which drew an estimated 325,000 people last year. Officials in Florida and Alabama also prepared emergency crews and urged residents to take precautions.“Obviously no need to panic at this point," Pensacola Mayor DC Reeves told a news conference. "This is really about preparation," Reeves added.
Article Summary: Tropical Storm Isaias formed Wednesday off eastern Mexico. Forecasters expect it to become a hurricane by Thursday as it turns north towards the Gulf Coast. A hurricane watch was issued for the northern Gulf Coast from Bay St. Louis, Mississippi, to Indian Pass on Florida’s Panhandle.

Article Title: Texas carries out first US execution since Christa Pike's botched lethal injection
Article Text:
File photo: Texas man executed for killing convenience store clerk in 2000

Texas executed Jamaal Howard, 46, on Wednesday, making him the first person put to death in the US since the botched execution of Christa Pike in Tennessee last week.Howard was pronounced dead at 8.03 pm after receiving a lethal dose of pentobarbital, a sedative, at the state prison in Huntsville.His lawyers had sought to halt the execution, arguing that Texas faced similar risks because it was using the same lethal injection drug involved in Pike’s failed execution. Pike survived two doses of pentobarbital and later said her arms felt as though they were going to explode as she was administered the drug.“Texas should not be eager to follow in Tennessee’s footsteps,” Howard’s lawyers argued in a motion filed before the Texas court of criminal appeals.The court rejected the request for a stay and later denied a second attempt to stop the execution over concerns about the drug. Both decisions came without explanation. The US Supreme Court also rejected a late appeal on Wednesday without comment.Howard was the sixth person executed in Texas this year and the 30th person put to death across the US in 2026. Two more lethal injections are scheduled in Texas.Howard was convicted of capital murder in 2001 for robbing a convenience store and fatally shooting 42-year-old store clerk Vickie Swartout.Before the execution, Howard apologised to members of Swartout’s family, who watched from a viewing room just feet from the death chamber.“I wish that you accept my apology and I wish for your forgiveness,” he said. “I’m sorry for what happened. I wish you can learn to forgive me one of these days.”His lawyers had also argued that Howard was intellectually disabled at the time of the crime and therefore ineligible for the death penalty under a 2002 US Supreme Court ruling.Howard’s lawyers cited Christa Pike’s case in their final appeal, arguing that Texas’ execution drugs could also have degraded because they were being used beyond their original beyond-use dates allowed under pharmaceutical standards.The Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals had declined a request to halt Howard’s execution last week.
Article Summary: Jamaal Howard was convicted of capital murder in 2001 for robbing a convenience store and fatally shooting 42-year-old store clerk Vickie Swartout. Howard was pronounced dead at 8.03 pm after receiving a lethal dose of pentobarbital, a sedative, at the state prison in Huntsville.

Article Title: Pentagon orders US military to gear up for Iran strikes; Trump yet to decide dates
Article Text:
The Pentagon has been instructed to prepare for possible military actions against Iran, amid stalled diplomatic efforts.

Situation in the Middle East

The Pentagon has instructed the US central command (CENTCOM) to complete preparations for a possible resumption of major combat operations against Iran. US President Donald Trump has not made a final decision yet on whether to launch fresh strikes, Axios reported, citing US officials.According to Axios, the preparations could pave the way for a new US military campaign targeting Iranian nuclear facilities, energy infrastructure and other strategic sites. However, the report said no timeline for an attack has been set and the Pentagon's preparations do not amount to a presidential order to begin strikes.The development comes as Washington's diplomatic efforts with Tehran remain deadlocked.Axios reported that negotiations have stalled, while a separate meeting of Trump's senior national-security team at Camp David last week focused on the Iran war and the escalating Saudi-Houthi conflict in Yemen. The meeting was chaired by Vice President JD Vance and included senior US defence, intelligence, diplomatic and economic officials.The timing is also linked to the US midterm elections and elections in Israel.Axios reported that US and Israeli officials are assessing the possibility of renewed operations before the elections, although an Israeli official said the chances of action before the polls are currently low and could rise after them.Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu have spoken twice in recent days. If fighting resumes, US and Israeli forces are expected to operate in tandem, while Israeli officials believe Iran could retaliate with ballistic-missile attacks against Israel.The Middle East is facing multiple connected fronts, with the US-Iran war now overlapping with renewed fighting in Yemen, direct Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia and continuing Israeli operations in Gaza and the wider region.Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces launched a major offensive against the Iran-backed Houthis earlier this week, seeking to retake territory along the Red Sea coast and around the strategic Bab el-Mandeb Strait.The Houthis have responded with missile and drone attacks against Saudi Arabia.
