Three people were killed and dozens wounded in attacks on Abha and Riyadh's King Khalid International airports, according to Saudi authorities cited by Reuters and AP. The Saudi-led coalition subsequently said it had struck more than 80 Houthi targets in Yemen.Israel is also heading towards elections on October 27, with the October 7, 2023 Hamas attack remaining a central issue in the campaign. AP reported that the election is increasingly being framed around responsibility for the security failure and Netanyahu's handling of the wars that followed.
Article Summary: US President Donald Trump has not made a final decision yet on whether to launch fresh strikes, Axios reported. The preparations could pave the way for a new US military campaign targeting Iranian nuclear facilities, energy infrastructure and other strategic sites. No timeline for an attack has been set and the Pentagon's preparations do not amount to a presidential order to begin strikes.

Article Title: Tulsa’s Arkansas River waterfront sat underused for years; billionaire George Kaiser put $465 million behind a 66-acre park that became a major public destination
Article Text:
PC: Forbes/Public Radio Tulsa

A neglected stretch of the Arkansas River gets a new purpose

George Kaiser put private wealth behind a public park

Playgrounds, trails and courts spread across the site

Gathering Place draws hundreds for its opening day in Tulsa

The park was designed around inclusion as well as recreation

The Arkansas River was once a difficult backdrop for Tulsa, with stretches of its waterfront offering little reason for residents to linger. That changed with the arrival of Gathering Place, a vast public park built with private funding and designed around recreation, culture and open space. Associated Press (AP) reported when it opened, the 66-acre first phase brought playgrounds, trails, sports facilities, lawns and gathering areas to the riverfront. The project was backed by the foundation of billionaire philanthropist George Kaiser, whose contribution helped finance a development that would eventually expand towards 100 acres. What began as an ambitious piece of urban redevelopment has since become one of Tulsa's most visited public spaces.Tulsa's relationship with the Arkansas River has not always been straightforward. The waterway runs through the city, but parts of its banks had long been underused, leaving a large amount of valuable urban space disconnected from everyday life.As reported by AP News, Gathering Place was conceived as a way of changing that. Rather than treating the riverfront simply as somewhere to pass through, the project put public activity at the centre of the design.The first phase covered about 66 acres, with plans for the park to eventually reach roughly 100 acres. The grounds were laid out for different kinds of use, from quiet walks and cycling to organised sport, concerts and family outings. The park was intended to work as a place people could visit for a few hours, but also as a setting for larger civic and cultural events.Gathering Place was built with private money, with major support coming from the George Kaiser Family Foundation. Kaiser, a Tulsa-born billionaire, had already become one of the city's most prominent philanthropists. His foundation's involvement gave the riverfront project access to a level of private funding rarely available for a conventional municipal park.The result was not simply a landscaped strip beside the river. The money went towards a substantial collection of facilities and public spaces, creating an environment intended to serve residents across different age groups and interests.Visitors arriving at Gathering Place encounter a park built around movement and activity rather than a single central attraction. There are walking and cycling routes, athletic courts and broad lawns that can accommodate concerts and other gatherings. Play areas were also a major part of the design, with children given dedicated spaces to climb, explore and play.The range of facilities means the park can feel different depending on when it is visited. A weekday morning might bring walkers and families, while evenings and weekends can draw larger crowds for performances and events.The river itself remains an important part of the setting. Instead of turning its back on Arkansas, the park incorporates the waterfront into the experience, making the landscape part of the attraction.When Gathering Place opened, hundreds of people gathered along the Tulsa riverfront to mark the occasion. The launch was designed as a public celebration rather than a conventional ribbon-cutting ceremony. A parade opened the day's programme, followed by live music and activities for children.Kaiser joined Oklahoma Gov. Mary Fallin and local officials for the opening, as residents explored a park that had taken years of planning and construction to reach that point. The crowds offered an early indication of how much interest the project had generated. For Tulsa, the opening also represented a significant change in how one of the city's major pieces of open land could be used.City leaders described Gathering Place as more than a collection of playgrounds, sports courts and green spaces. The project was also presented as an experiment in creating a public setting where people from different parts of the city could meet. That ambition influenced the range of spaces included in the park. There are areas intended for active recreation, quieter corners, performance spaces and facilities aimed at families.The emphasis on accessibility and broad public use was particularly important because the park had been financed privately. Its purpose was not to create an exclusive development around the river, but a public destination available to people without an admission charge.
Article Summary: Gathering Place was built with private money, with major support coming from the George Kaiser Family Foundation. The first phase covered about 66 acres, with plans for the park to eventually reach roughly 100 acres. The park was intended to work as a place people could visit for a few hours, but also as a setting for larger civic and cultural events.

Article Title: This Arizona ranch spans 114,000 acres and has stayed with one family for nearly 80 years; now it is listed for $43 million
Article Text:
Representative Image of Marley Ranch’s Sonoran Desert grasslands with mountains under a blue sky ( AI Generrated Image)

A 114,000-acre ranch with 1,600-cattle capacity

The ranch stretches across 2 Arizona counties

A Marley family property since the 1940s

A sprawling stretch of the Sonoran Desert that has remained in the same family for nearly 80 years is now on the market for $43 million. According to Mansion Global, Marley Ranch, located between Tucson and Nogales in southern Arizona, spans more than 114,000 acres within its ranch boundary and is being offered for the first time in more than 75 years. The ranch has been in the Marley family's ownership since Kemper and Ethel Marley established it in the 1940s and later expanded it. It includes rolling grasslands surrounded by high mountains and sits on the west side of the Santa Cruz River, an area associated with the routes of Spanish conquistadors and the missionary Father Kino. The property can accommodate up to 1,600 cattle, although the cattle and ranch equipment are not included in the asking price.Marley Ranch spans 114,279.48 acres, equivalent to 178.56 sections, according to the current property listing. However, the entire acreage is not privately owned land. The ranch consists of 17,265.07 acres of deeded land alongside land held through several grazing arrangements, including a large Arizona State Land Department grazing lease, a Bureau of Land Management allotment, private grazing licenses and leases, and Pima County land.The listing says the ranch has a carrying capacity of 1,600 animal units during normal rainfall years, although actual use varies depending on rainfall. Mansion Global similarly reports that the ranch can accommodate up to 1,600 head of cattle. The animals and equipment are separate from the $43 million sale price. The property is built around an extensive cattle operation. It has 28 major pastures, several large working corrals, smaller branding corrals and traps, as well as 60 dirt stock ponds. Its water infrastructure includes 19 stock wells, of which 15 are operating, along with 4 domestic wells and 2 grandfathered irrigation wells. Ten of the ranch's wells are solar-powered. More than 52 miles of pipeline, with storage and troughs, help distribute water across the property.The Marley Cattle Company is located in southern Arizona's Sonoran Desert, about 20 miles south of Tucson and near Amado. The ranch lies west of Interstate 19, with the headquarters located along Arivaca Road in Santa Cruz County and another homestead area in Pima County. The property is roughly 20 miles wide from east to west and about 15 miles from north to south on its western side, according to the listing. The ranch's elevation ranges from about 3,109 feet above sea level at the homestead to 4,700 feet in the Colorado Mountains, with most of the property between 3,200 and 3,800 feet. The listing describes the ranch as being on the west side of the Santa Cruz River, which it identifies as a historic route associated with Spanish conquistadors and Father Kino.Despite its size, the ranch is equipped for a working cattle operation rather than being simply undeveloped desert acreage. Its headquarters includes a ranch manager's double-wide mobile home, 3 small ranch-hand houses, another mobile home, a shop, hay shed, tack room, covered horse pens, shipping corrals with a scale and a feed yard. At the separate homestead, the listing includes an owner's residence and bunkhouses that are currently non-habitable, along with a guest house and a residence occupied by ranch hands. There is also a dirt airstrip at the homestead that, when maintained, can accommodate twin-engine aircraft. The ranch is fenced around its perimeter, while roads across the property are maintained by the ranch.The ranch's history stretches back to Kemper and Ethel Marley, who acquired land in the 1940s and expanded the property. According to Mansion Global, the couple made their primary home in Phoenix but were closely involved in ranch life, including riding with crews during cattle roundups. Kemper Marley, who built a business empire that included cattle farms and other companies, died in 1990 at age 83. Ethel Marley died in 1997 at age 90.The ranch remained with the Marley family after their deaths. Mansion Global reports that it was eventually turned over to their 3 nephews, while the current generation did not want to continue owning the property. The current listing describes the ranch as being offered for sale for the first time in more than 75 years, making the $43 million listing a significant change for a property that has remained associated with the Marley family for decades. Mansion Global reported that Marley Ranch is one of the most expensive listings in Arizona and described it as the state's most expensive ranch listing at the time of its March 2026 report. The current listing price remains $43 million, with the cattle and equipment excluded from the sale.
Article Summary: Marley Ranch spans 114,279.48 acres, equivalent to 178.56 sections, according to the current property listing. The ranch has been in the Marley family's ownership since Kemper and Ethel Marley established it in the 1940s and later expanded it. It includes rolling grasslands surrounded by high mountains and sits on the west side of the Santa Cruz River, an area associated with the routes of Spanish conquistadors and Father Kino.

Article Title: Pakistan bets on electric vehicles as Middle East war sends petrol prices soaring 54%
Article Text:
Pakistan fuel prices to be revised every day

EV sales accelerate amid fuel price pressure

Pakistan expects to achieve its electric-vehicle adoption target ahead of schedule as surging oil prices make the shift away from petrol-powered vehicles increasingly attractive, a senior government official said.The government aims for electric vehicles to account for 30% of new vehicle sales by 2030 under its EV policy announced last year. Haroon Akhtar, adviser to Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on industries and production, said the sharp rise in fuel prices has reduced the time needed for buyers to recover the higher upfront cost of EVs.“I feel that the target we had set in our electric-vehicle policy last year, we will achieve it much earlier as rise in oil prices has brought cost recovery of EV to one to one and a half year,” Akhtar told Bloomberg in Islamabad.“People are realizing the benefit now. You don't have to pay for petrol,” he said.Petrol and diesel prices in Pakistan have risen 54% and 43%, respectively, since the Middle East conflict began in February, according to data available from Pakistan State Oil Company Ltd.Akhtar said sales of electric motorcycles and scooters have tripled from a year earlier, while electric-car sales have doubled, although industry-wide EV sales data is not publicly available.“This is an impact of the Middle East conflict, as fuel prices have gone up,” Akhtar said.Despite the growing incentive to switch to EVs, factors including high vehicle costs and limited charging infrastructure mean a large-scale transformation of Pakistan’s vehicle fleet and oil consumption will take years.The government is also preparing a new auto policy that could be presented to the cabinet within the next two weeks. It is considering tax incentives for EVs to narrow the price gap between electric and conventional vehicles, Akhtar said.
Article Summary: Pakistan aims for electric vehicles to account for 30% of new vehicle sales by 2030. The sharp rise in fuel prices has reduced the time needed for buyers to recover the higher upfront cost of EVs. The government is also preparing a new auto policy that could be presented to the cabinet within the next two weeks.

Article Title: Pakistan-Afghanistan conflict: A clash of unequals, but why is Islamabad relying on air power instead of ground offensive
Article Text:
Pakistan has been conducting air strikes against alleged TTP hideouts in Afghanistan

Pakistan and Afghanistan: Tensions despite cultural ties

Taliban doesn't recognise the Durand Line

Pakistan and Afghanistan: A clash of unequals

PAF has an inventory of several advanced fighter aircraft

Pakistan has overwhelming military advantage over Afghanistan

Imposing costs, not capturing territory

PAF is world's seventh-largest air force

A ‘graveyard of empires’

Poll Vote & Share your view Should Pakistan consider launching a ground offensive in Afghanistan? Yes, to combat the TTP effectively No, air strikes are sufficient 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

The human and financial cost of a ground war

Air power: Pakistan’s strategic calculus?

Pakistan and Afghanistan have, over the years, repeatedly exchanged fire along their international border, including in clashes since October last year.Pakistan has overwhelming military superiority over the Taliban regime. Yet, as in previous periods of conflict, Islamabad has stopped short of launching a full-scale ground offensive into Afghanistan. Instead, it has relied primarily on air strikes against targets inside Afghan territory.This raises a central question: why has Pakistan relied on air power rather than launching a ground offensive in Afghanistan?The two countries are more than immediate neighbours. They share deep ties rooted in religion, ethnicity, food and social traditions. Pakistan is also home to a large population of Afghan refugees and asylum seekers. According to the UNHCR, around 1.5 million Afghans were living in Pakistan as of early 2025, most displaced by decades of war, political instability and economic hardship.Yet these longstanding ties have not prevented repeated clashes along the Durand Line, the Pakistan-Afghanistan border that the Taliban does not recognise. The current tensions are particularly notable given that Islamabad initially reached out to the Taliban after the hardline Islamist movement once again seized power in Afghanistan, within days of US-led coalition troops completing their withdrawal in 2021 after nearly two decades in the country.The current conflict, like previous episodes of tension, centres on Islamabad’s allegation that elements hostile to Pakistan operate from Afghan territory — in this case, specifically the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP). Kabul denies the allegation and has accused Pakistan of attacking Afghan civilians.On October 9, 2025, the Pakistan Air Force (PAF) struck several alleged TTP hideouts in Afghanistan, prompting a Taliban retaliation. Intermittent fighting has continued since, with Pakistan relying on air power against what it describes as TTP targets inside Afghanistan.The Taliban’s lack of an air force is one of the first reasons cited for Pakistan’s preference for air strikes inside Afghanistan. This gives the PAF, the world’s seventh-largest air force, the ability to hit targets inside Afghanistan and return to Pakistani airspace safely and swiftly.Yet air power is only one dimension of the stark disparity in military power between Islamabad and Kabul.According to the Global Firepower Index, Pakistan is a top-15 military power, ranking 14th among 145 countries. It also possesses nuclear weapons, making it one of only nine countries — and the only Muslim-majority state — to have nuclear bombs.Unsurprisingly, Afghanistan features among the lowest-ranked countries on the Global Firepower Index, at 121st. Taliban fighters rely largely on military equipment left behind by the departed US-led coalition forces and the former Afghan army that operated under the Washington-backed civilian governments of Hamid Karzai and, later, Ashraf Ghani. The Taliban also deploy guerrilla warfare tactics to fight their adversaries.Given this stark imbalance, air power also helps Islamabad avoid the optics of a stronger state invading or seeking to capture territory from a weaker adversary, as would be the case with a land offensive.The PAF also offers Pakistan distinct operational advantages beyond the simple fact that Afghanistan lacks air power.Pakistani analysts argue that the objective is to impose significant costs on the TTP rather than capture Afghan territory. Pakistan can therefore conduct precision strikes deep inside Afghanistan without deploying ground forces, hitting individuals it describes as terrorists without taking on the far greater commitment of a ground operation.Air power also allows Islamabad to limit the scale of its operations while simultaneously signalling its intent. The PAF can carry out limited strikes against specific targets and then disengage, rather than becoming drawn into a sustained military campaign.A ground offensive, on the other hand, could risk turning the conflict into a full-scale war, with potentially far greater political and diplomatic consequences for Pakistan, including increased international pressure and the possibility of sanctions.Afghanistan is often described as a “graveyard of empires”, a relatively modern moniker referring to how major powers have failed in establishing and sustaining control over the country. Among them are the British, the Soviet Union and, more recently, the United States.That narrative is rooted partly in the geographical challenges posed by the region’s rugged and mountainous terrain. The Hindu Kush mountain range runs across much of Afghanistan, while the Safed Koh range extends along parts of its eastern border with Pakistan.According to experts, such terrain not only makes it difficult for conventional forces to move through and hold territory, but also provides favourable conditions for guerrilla warfare.Hence, this works in favour of the Taliban, which, in addition to its knowledge of local geography, has decades of experience fighting militarily superior adversaries through guerrilla and other asymmetric tactics. The group could inflict significant casualties on Pakistani troops while making it harder for Islamabad to sustain a ground offensive in unfamiliar and difficult terrain. Pakistan could therefore face a prolonged campaign against combatants well versed in hit-and-run attacks.Air power presents a fundamentally different proposition. With aerial strikes, Pakistan can hit locations inside Afghanistan without requiring large numbers of soldiers to physically enter and hold the terrain. While mountainous geography can also pose challenges for the air force, Islamabad could still avoid the far greater logistical and military burden of a ground campaign.For Pakistan, a ground offensive would also come with significant human, financial and logistical costs. The experience of the US-led Operation Enduring Freedom in Afghanistan illustrates how a campaign that began with overwhelming military superiority eventually evolved into a prolonged conflict. Between 2001 and 2021, the United States spent an estimated $2.26 trillion on the war in Afghanistan, according to Brown University’s Costs of War project.But the financial burden was only one part of the toll. The US lost 2,461 service members during the two-decade conflict, while thousands more were wounded. The war also required a sustained deployment of troops, extensive logistical networks and significant resources to maintain military operations thousands of kilometres from the United States.For Pakistan, with its struggling economy, the financial burden of sustaining a prolonged ground campaign would be significant. Analysts agree that neither side has the “will or capacity to engage in protracted wars.”Logistically, Pakistan, as an immediate neighbour of Afghanistan, would not face the same geographical and financial burdens as the United States. Nevertheless, a ground offensive would require Islamabad to deploy and sustain troops inside Afghan territory, protect supply lines and military positions, and potentially absorb casualties over an extended period. The longer such an operation continued, the greater the demands on Pakistan’s military and economy would become.Against these costs, air strikes offer Islamabad a way to pursue its military objectives without committing to the financial and logistical demands of a prolonged ground campaign.For Pakistan, the choice between air power and ground forces ultimately comes down to the nature of the response it wants to mount. Air strikes allow it to respond to developments along its Afghan border without fundamentally changing the character of the confrontation. A ground offensive, on the other hand, could trigger a major escalation, with consequences extending well beyond the battlefield.This distinction may help explain why Pakistan has so far stopped short of sending ground troops into Afghanistan.For now, therefore, Islamabad appears to be pursuing a strategy of pressure without occupation. Whether this can produce the desired changes in the behaviour of the Taliban — or even the TTP — remains an open question. But its continued preference for air strikes suggests that Pakistan sees value in keeping the confrontation limited rather than allowing it to develop into a wider war.
Article Summary: Pakistani analysts argue that the objective is to impose significant costs on the TTP rather than capture Afghan territory. Pakistan can therefore conduct precision strikes deep inside Afghanistan without deploying ground forces. Air power also helps Islamabad avoid the optics of a stronger state invading or seeking to capture territory.

Article Title: Pakistan forces accused of quadcopter blast that killed 2 children in Balochistan
Article Text:
Pakistan forces accused of quadcopter link

A blast in Balochistan's Panjgur district killed two children and left three others injured, The Balochistan Post reported. The incident took place in Fateh Ali Bazaar in Gowargo tehsil, where the children had been playing.According to the report, the children noticed an unidentified object hanging from a tree. The object exploded after it was disturbed, killing two boys aged nine and 10. Three other boys, aged seven, nine and 12, were injured.The nature of the device that caused the explosion remains unclear.However, local sources alleged that it was connected to a quadcopter operated by Pakistani security forces. One source also claimed that explosives had been attached to a military quadcopter and placed in the area.The source further alleged that local journalists were later told to describe the incident as a hand-grenade blast or an explosion involving another device.The Panjgur incident comes amid other allegations of civilian casualties involving military drones and quadcopters in Balochistan.On September 24, four young men were killed and two others injured in an alleged military drone strike in Balicha, Kech, according to The Balochistan Post.Families of those killed said the men had gone there for a picnic and denied claims that they were militants.The incident triggered a boycott of courts across Makran, while lawyers called for an independent probe into the deaths.Earlier on September 18, five civilians were reportedly injured in alleged quadcopter attacks in Balochabad and Bullo in the Mand area, the report said.
Article Summary: Blast in Balochistan's Panjgur district killed two children and left three others injured. Local sources alleged that it was connected to a quadcopter operated by Pakistani security forces. Incident comes amid other allegations of civilian casualties involving military drones and quadcopters.

Article Title: Nearly 3 in 4 Pakistan inmates await trial amid prison overcrowding in country: Report
Article Text:
73% of Pakistan prisoners are under-trial, HRCP report finds

Poll Vote & Share your view What do you think is the main cause of prison overcrowding in Pakistan? Delays in the justice system Arbitrary arrests Weak bail procedures Other reasons 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Pakistan's prisons are facing severe overcrowding, with people awaiting trial making up nearly three-fourths of the country's prison population, a Human Rights Commission of Pakistan (HRCP) report has found.The report, 'Beyond the Prison Wall: Reducing Overcrowding in Pakistan's Prisons', said 73.41% of inmates were under-trial in 2024. The share has gone up from 66% in 2017, The Express Tribune reported.The report said Pakistan's prisons were operating at 152.2% of their approved capacity on average during July and August 2024.The HRCP said simply building more prisons would not address the problem. It pointed to delays in the justice system, including lengthy trials, weak bail procedures and the widespread use of pre-trial detention.Punjab faces an even bigger problem. According to official figures cited by the HRCP, 74,773 prisoners were held in 45 prisons across the province in September 2026. The sanctioned capacity was 39,204, meaning the prisons were operating at nearly 191% of capacity.Of the total inmates, 54,932 were awaiting trial.Punjab has added new prisons, barracks and other facilities over the years, but the report said the additional capacity has not matched the rise in the number of prisoners.The scale of the problem has grown majorly. Punjab province had 52,803 prisoners against a capacity of 21,527 in 2010. Overcrowding in the province stood at 173.6% in 2024, according to figures cited by The Express Tribune.The HRCP blamed arbitrary arrests, delays in investigations and lengthy prosecution for the growing number of people held without conviction.As a result, many accused people remain behind bars for months or even years while waiting for investigations and court proceedings to move forward, the report said.
Article Summary: 73.41% of inmates in Pakistan's prisons were under-trial in 2024. The share has gone up from 66% in 2017, according to a Human Rights Commission of Pakistan report. The HRCP said simply building more prisons would not address the problem. Delays in the justice system, arbitrary arrests and weak bail procedures were blamed.

Article Title: 'Come to your senses': What is Pakistan PM Shehbaz Sharif's condition for talks with Imran's party
Article Text:
Shehbaz’s talks offer fails to sway PTI as long march presses on

Poll Vote & Share your view Do you think dialogue is the best way to resolve political disagreements? Yes, dialogue can help No, other steps are needed It depends on the situation 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Imran Khan-led Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) on Tuesday questioned the seriousness of Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif ’s offer for talks, calling it "merely symbolic" and saying the government had taken no concrete step beyond extending the invitation, Pakistan Today reported.PTI spokesperson Gohar said the Shehbaz Sharif-led government had also prevented PTI leaders from meeting the party’s founder and former PM Imran Khan , for nearly a year.Speaking to reporters in Rawalpindi, he said the last such meeting took place in October last year, Geo News reported.His remarks came after Sharif asked PTI to halt its ongoing long march towards Islamabad as a condition for holding talks.At an event in Islamabad, the prime minister warned that protests and long marches could hurt Pakistan’s economy. "I urge you to come to your senses, end the long march and sit-in, and then we will sit with you," he said.The PTI-led march, meanwhile, continued towards Peshawar on Monday, with Khyber Pakhtunkhwa chief minister Sohail Afridi calling on party supporters to join the mobilisation.Afridi addressed march participants after the convoy reached Kohat and thanked residents for their "magnificent welcome". He said the convoy would resume its journey towards Peshawar from University Chowk on Tuesday, The Express Tribune reported.Declaring his loyalty to Imran Khan, Afridi said, “I am a soldier of Imran Khan. Even if the whole world comes together, it cannot put a price on me." He also urged supporters to send a message that Khyber Pakhtunkhwa belongs to Imran Khan.The chief minister had started the march from Lakki Marwat on Sunday after negotiations between PTI and the federal government failed to settle differences over the planned protest.Those talks, led by national assembly speaker Ayaz Sadiq, ended on Saturday without an agreement.The Pakistan government had asked PTI to call off the march, while the opposition sought assurances that its leaders would be permitted to meet long-imprisoned Imran Khan.
Article Summary: Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif asked PTI to halt its long march towards Islamabad as a condition for holding talks. PTI spokesperson said government had taken no concrete step beyond extending invitation. Khyber Pakhtunkhwa chief minister Sohail Afridi called on supporters to join mobilisation.

Article Title: Pakistan successfully test-fires extended version of Fatah-4 cruise missile
Article Text:
Senior Pakistan army officers, together with scientists and engineers, were reportedly present to watch the launch.

Pakistan successfully test-fired its homemade extended version of the ground-based Fatah-4 cruise missile on Tuesday.The cruise missile is capable of engaging long-range targets with high precision, the army said. PTI reported.In a statement, Pakistan Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR) said the “weapon system is capable of engaging targets at extended ranges with high precision and lethality.”According to the Pakistan army, the test validated additional technical parameters of various sub-systems incorporated for improved accuracy and enhanced survivability.Senior Pakistan army officers, together with scientists and engineers, were reportedly present to watch the launch.President Asif Ali Zardari , Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif , Field Marshal Asim Munir, who serves as Chief of Army Staff and Chief of Defence Forces, and the services chiefs praised the successful test.Pakistan had previously carried out a successful test of the Fatah-IV ground-launched cruise missile in May.The base version of Fatah-4 reportedly has a range of up to 750 kilometres and can reportedly hit targets with a five-metre accuracy.The military confirmed the new variant has an extended range but did not clarify how far.Fatah-4 is a conventional cruise missile of Islamabad’s army rocket force command. It flies at an altitude of about 50 meters to evade air defences and avoid radar detection.
Article Summary: Pakistan successfully test-fired its homemade extended version of the ground- based Fatah-4 cruise missile on Tuesday. Senior Pakistan army officers, together with scientists and engineers, were reportedly present to watch the launch. President Asif Ali Zardari, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, Field Marshal Asim Munir and the services chiefs praised the successful test.

Article Title: Another showdown brewing in Pakistan? Imran Khan supporters hit streets after talks fail
Article Text:
Supporters of imprisoned Imran Khan march towards Islamabad demanding his release.

Talks between PTI, government fail

Poll Vote & Share your view How do you feel about the government response to the PTI protests? It's appropriate and necessary. It's excessive and unjustified. 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Thousands of supporters of jailed former Pakistan prime minister Imran Khan began a march towards Islamabad on Sunday, demanding his release after talks between his Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party and the government failed to break the political deadlock.Khan, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif's main political rival, has been in prison since 2023 on corruption and other charges. Khan and his party have described the cases as politically motivated, the Associated Press reported.Despite his imprisonment, he continues to command a large and committed support base.The protesters set off from Lakki Marwat district in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, where PTI is in power, in a convoy of trucks, buses and cars. Organisers have planned overnight stops as the caravan makes its way towards Islamabad.Khyber Pakhtunkhwa chief minister Sohail Afridi, a staunch Khan supporter, is leading the march. Speaking from a specially designed container truck bearing a large portrait of Khan, Afridi expressed confidence that the movement would succeed in taking its demands to the heart of the capital.Authorities have erected roadblocks using shipping containers at entry points to Islamabad and at several locations inside the city.PTI and the federal government had held talks over postponing the march, but failed to reach an agreement. PTI chairman Gohar Khan said negotiations remained deadlocked after two rounds.Interior minister Mohsin Naqvi blamed Afridi for the failure of the talks and warned that he would be held responsible for any loss of life during the planned march.The government had urged PTI to postpone the protest, citing a rise in militant attacks by the Pakistani Taliban, also known as Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), in the northwest. The government has also accused PTI of sympathising with the TTP.PTI organisers, however, have vowed to reach Islamabad after mobilising hundreds of thousands of Khan supporters. Apart from Khan's release, protesters are demanding that he be shifted to a hospital and that his family be allowed to visit him.Officials have said Khan is in good health and receives regular family visits, but maintain that meetings with the imprisoned former prime minister cannot be used for political purposes.The march was originally scheduled for September 27 but was postponed after PTI leaders said authorities had blocked key routes to Islamabad, including the Attock Bridge, a major crossing used by convoys from Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.Previous protests by Khan's supporters have turned violent. During one such protest in 2024, security personnel and civilians were killed.
Article Summary: Talks between PTI, government fail to break political deadlock. Protesters set off from Lakki Marwat district in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, where PTI is in power, in a convoy of trucks, buses and cars. Khan has been in prison since 2023 on corruption and other charges.

Article Title: Pakistan braces for showdown as talks collapse, Imran Khan’s party pushes ahead with march
Article Text:
Imran Khan has been incarcerated since 2023.

PTI demands access to Imran Khan

Government and PTI blame each other

Long march to begin from Khyber Pakhtunkhwa

Poll Vote & Share your view Should the federal government negotiate further with PTI? Yes, dialogue is essential No, they should stand firm Only under certain conditions 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Pakistan’s opposition Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party will proceed with its planned long march towards Islamabad after a second round of talks with the government ended without a deal on access to jailed former prime minister Imran Khan The negotiations began at 4 pm on Saturday and continued into the early hours of Sunday, but the two sides failed to resolve their differences. The main dispute centred on PTI’s demand for an immediate meeting with Khan, including access to his personal doctor.PTI had initially planned to start the long march on September 27 but postponed it to October 4 after the federal government introduced measures aimed at preventing the protest.The party wants an immediate meeting with Khan and has demanded that he be taken to a hospital where his personal doctors can examine him.Khan, 73, has been in jail since 2023 after being convicted in a corruption case. He is currently held at the high-security Adiala Jail in Rawalpindi.PTI has also called for the release of Khan’s sisters and other people arrested ahead of the protest. It wants a proper medical examination of Khan’s wife, Bushra Bibi, and has demanded that their legal cases be heard without interference.The government, however, insisted that PTI first cancel the protest before it would consider allowing its leaders to meet Khan, according to sources. PTI rejected that condition and wanted access to its jailed leader before deciding whether to call off the march.Tehreek-e-Tahafuz-e-Ayin-e-Pakistan leader Senator Allama Nasir Abbas said the negotiations had failed because the two sides could not agree on the roles of the federal and provincial governments in dealing with terrorism in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, as well as access to Khan.“No understanding could be reached regarding the respective roles of the province and the federal government concerning terrorism in the province, and the matter of a meeting with Imran Khan remains unresolved,” Abbas, who is also Leader of the Opposition in the Senate, said.“We endeavoured to reach a conclusion, but the deadlock persists -- specifically regarding access to Khan Sahib's personal physician,” he added.Minister of State for Interior Tallal Chaudhry said the talks failed mainly because the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa government could not guarantee that it would cooperate with the federal government in the fight against terrorism in the future.Khyber Pakhtunkhwa is governed by PTI, and the province is also where the planned march will begin.Pakistan Peoples Party leader Sherry Rehman, who took part in the negotiations, said the government delegation had discussed all the opposition's demands.“Unfortunately, the draft [agreement] was changed four times after it was agreed upon,” she told Geo News, adding that she would not go into the details.Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Chief Minister Sohail Afridi announced at 12:46 am that the protest would go ahead.He said supporters from Tank, Dera Ismail Khan, South Waziristan, North Waziristan, Bannu and Lakki Marwat would join the march at Gandi Chowk in Lakki Marwat at 1 pm on Sunday.The convoy is scheduled to stop near Karak for the night before leaving at 12:30 pm the following day and staying overnight near Kohat.On October 6, protesters from Kohat, Hangu, Kurram and Orakzai will join the convoy as it moves towards Peshawar, with the group expected to spend the night near Mattani.Afridi said the caravan would leave Budh Bair in Peshawar on the afternoon of October 7. Supporters from other parts of Peshawar will join at Kohat Road Bridge and the Motorway Toll Plaza before the convoy moves towards Charsadda.“The remaining constituencies of Peshawar will join us at Kohat Road Bridge and the Motorway Toll Plaza. And we will spend the night near Charsadda Interchange,” he said.The protesters are scheduled to leave Charsadda Interchange at 12:30 pm on October 8 after supporters from Charsadda and Mohmand join them.Afridi said people from across Khyber Pakhtunkhwa would gather at Khairabad later that day before the next stage of the march is announced.“God willing, the plan for the next phase will be announced there,” he said.The federal government has warned that the protesters will not be allowed to enter Islamabad. Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif ’s political adviser Rana Sanaullah said authorities would prevent the march from reaching the capital.“No one would be allowed to enter Islamabad,” he told reporters.The government had earlier said it would block roads leading into Islamabad with shipping containers and deploy additional security personnel to prevent the protesters from entering the capital.
Article Summary: Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party will proceed with its planned long march towards Islamabad. The party wants an immediate meeting with Khan and has demanded that he be taken to a hospital where his personal doctors can examine him. The government, however, insisted that PTI first cancel the protest before it would consider allowing its leaders to meet Khan.

Article Title: India slams Pakistan at UN, says ‘so-called’ civilian governments serve at army’s mercy
Article Text:
Pakistan's Prime Minister Muhammad Shehbaz Sharif

India on Friday hit back at Pakistan at the UN General Assembly, rejecting Islamabad’s remarks on Jammu and Kashmir and accusing its “so-called” civilian governments of serving “at the mercy” of the army.Exercising its Right of Reply during a Third Committee meeting, first secretary at the Permanent Mission of India to the UN Bhavika Mangalanandan said Pakistan’s civilian governments “rarely complete their terms”, while accusing Islamabad of using cross-border terrorism to divert attention from domestic discontent.Accoridng to news agency PTI, India “categorically” rejected Pakistan’s remarks on Jammu and Kashmir, asserting that the Union Territories of Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh were, are and will always remain “integral and inalienable” parts of India.“We all know that the so-called civilian governments in Pakistan serve at the mercy of their army and rarely complete their terms,” Mangalanandan said.Referring to jailed former Pakistan prime minister Imran Khan, she said a “former Prime Minister continues to remain in jail, even as his health is reported to be fast deteriorating.”She also said the erstwhile ruling party had not been allowed to contest elections.“Instead of addressing domestic discontent, Pakistan seeks to distract by fomenting instability in India and sponsoring, inciting, abetting, and financing cross-border terrorism in my country for more than three decades,” she said.Turning to Jammu and Kashmir, Mangalanandan said, “The only outstanding matter is a vacation of the territory Pakistan holds under illegal and forcible occupation.She accused Pakistan of attempting to divert attention from unrest in the country.“This is a desperate attempt by Pakistan to mask the ongoing tragedy in Rawalakot and its other cities, the killing of hundreds of civilians, and the brutal crackdown across Pakistan-occupied Jammu and Kashmir, for merely demanding bread, electricity and human dignity,” she said.India also invoked the term “Form 47”, used in reference to allegations of rigging and manipulation in Pakistan’s 2024 general elections.“When any free media is banned from covering such news in Pakistan, the evidence becomes undeniable for the global community that only the writ of the Form 47 government and their masters and the army headquarters runs large,” she said.Contrasting this with Jammu and Kashmir, India said Assembly Elections were held there in 2024, followed by a peaceful transfer of power to an elected government.“The contrast could not have been starker. The only human rights violation taking place in Kashmir is perpetrated by the armed forces of Pakistan and their terrorist proxies. Propaganda does not become fact through repetition,” Mangalanandan said.“Pakistan would serve its people better by confronting its own fault lines and building its economy than by coveting the territory of others,” she added.
Article Summary: India “categorically” rejected Pakistan’s remarks on Jammu and Kashmir, asserting that the Union Territories of Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh were, are and will always remain “integral and inalienable”

Article Title: Pakistan kills 5 TTP militants as violence escalates on Afghanistan border
Article Text:
The militants reportedly belonged to Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan, which the government calls Fitna al-Khawarij (Representative image: Reuters).

Pakistani security forces killed five militants during an intelligence-based operation on Saturday in the country's Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province.The militants reportedly belonged to Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan , which the government calls Fitna al-Khawarij.The operation was carried out in KPK's South Waziristan district, based on intelligence about several militant hideouts, PTI reported, citing an official.A large quantity of weapons and ammunition was also recovered, the official said.Pak army has been targeting such hideouts amid increased violence at the Afghanistan border.On Friday, seven militants belonging to the same group were killed in North Waziristan district. Such operations form part of Pakistan's Azm-e-Istehkam initiative, aimed at countering terrorism.Khyber Pakhtunkhwa has long struggled with instability, fueled by militant violence, the movement of fighters across the border from Afghanistan, and repeated military campaigns.After its ceasefire agreement with the Pakistani government collapsed in November 2022, the TTP has launched a series of attacks in the province, which borders Afghanistan.Last week, a suicide bombing at a roadside police checkpoint in KPK's Dera Ismail Khan district killed more than a dozen security personnel and wounded at least 30 others. Nearly 21 people died in the city of Kohat after a car loaded with explosives rammed into the entrance of a mosque; both attacks were linked to the TTP.According to the Centre for Research and Security Studies, an Islamabad-based think tank, KPK was Pakistan's worst-hit region for violence in the third quarter of 2025. The region recorded around 638 violence-related deaths, nearly 71 per cent of the national total. KPK also faced 221 violent incidents, more than 67 per cent of the total.Overall, Pakistan recorded 1,232 rebel group attacks during the first nine months of 2026, according to a report by the Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies, with the number of attacks in September reaching a 12-year high.
Article Summary: Militants reportedly belonged to Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan, which the government calls Fitna al-Khawarij. Operation carried out in KPK's South Waziristan district, based on intelligence about several militant hideouts. A large quantity of weapons and ammunition was also recovered.

Article Title: Pakistan logs over 1.2k rebel attacks in 9 months of ’26, security crisis deepens
Article Text: During the first nine months of 2026, Pakistan recorded 1,232 rebel group attacks, according to a report by Islamabad-based think tank Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies, indicating that a major security crisis is brewing. The number of attacks in Sept reached a 12-year high, with 225 attacks resulting in 545 deaths. Police and military personnel have been the primary targets of these operations, accounting for majority of fatalities.Spearheaded by groups such as Tehrik-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), Baloch Liberation Army, Baloch Liberation Front and alliances like Ittehad Mujahideen Pakistan, these attacks remain concentrated in Balochistan and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, and former tribal areas. Formed in 2025, IMP is the latest threat and comprises three sub-outfits — Hafiz Gul Bahadur group (HGBG), Lashkar-e-Islam and Harakat Inqilab-e-Islami Pakistan.Just last week, over a dozen security personnel were killed and at least 30 wounded in a suicide bombing at a roadside police checkpoint in Dera Ismail Khan district of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province. A week before that around 21 Pakistani security personnel were killed and dozens injured in a powerful suicide bombing and subsequent firing at the police line and intelligence facility in Kohat, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.The surge in Sept represents a 13% increase from 199 incidents reported in Aug, marking the third consecutive month of compounding violence.Balochistan served as the primary epicentre of the escalation, bearing the brunt of the violence with 131 recorded attacks, accounting for more than half of all nationwide incidents. Khyber Pakhtunkhwa followed with 58 attacks, while the former tribal areas recorded 34 incidents, the institute claimed. Tensions between Islamabad and Kabul have risen as Pakistan repeatedly accuses the ruling Afghan Taliban of providing safe havens and operational freedom to the TTP.
Article Summary: During the first nine months of 2026, Pakistan recorded 1,232 rebel group attacks. The number of attacks in Sept reached a 12-year high, with 225 attacks resulting in 545 deaths. Police and military personnel have been the primary targets of these operations.

Article Title: Shehbaz govt, Imran Khan’s PTI hold talks as Pakistan braces for protests
Article Text: Pakistan’s federal government and jailed former prime minister Imran Khan ’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) agreed to hold a second round of talks on Saturday, as the opposition party prepares for a long march towards Islamabad from October 4.The first round of negotiations was held on Friday in the chamber of national assembly speaker Sardar Ayaz Sadiq, who is facilitating the dialogue amid heightened security in the capital.According to a statement issued by the National Assembly Secretariat, the participants held detailed discussions “on the prevailing political situation and exchanged views on various matters of national importance”.“The government, PPP and opposition representatives apprised each other of their respective positions and held a detailed exchange of views constructively and cordially. The participants emphasised the need to resolve national issues through dialogue and negotiations,” it said, according to news agency PTI.The second round will be held at 2 pm on Saturday in the speaker’s chamber.Sadiq said he was “only playing the role of a mediator”, adding that his office was “always open” to resolving issues through negotiations.“Parliament is the only forum where solutions to issues can be found,” he said, stressing that negotiations were the way to address political differences.PTI international spokesman Zulfiqar Bukhari said the talks were “primarily aimed at defusing the current political situation surrounding PTI’s planned march/protest toward Islamabad on October 4”.Bukhari said the party’s demands included an “immediate” meeting with Khan and a decision to take him to hospital so his personal doctors could examine him. PTI has also sought the release of Khan’s sisters and others arrested ahead of the protest, a medical check-up for his wife Bushra Bibi and proper hearings in their cases.Meanwhile, the Pakistan authorities have deployed additional police and placed shipping containers on routes into Islamabad. The blockades have already disrupted freight movement.Bukhari said the long march would begin from Gandi Chowk in Lakki Marwat, with stops planned in Karak and Kohat on October 5 before entering Peshawar district.
Article Summary: Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf to hold second round of talks on Saturday. Opposition party preparing for long march towards Islamabad from October 4. First round of negotiations was held on Friday in the chamber of national assembly speaker Sardar Ayaz Sadiq.

Article Title: 'Vague and broad': UN experts slam Pakistan's counter-terrorism laws, demand release of lawyer couple
Article Text:
UN experts demand release of Pakistani lawyers, question terror laws

United Nations human rights experts have stepped up pressure on Pakistan to release Pakistani lawyers Imaan Mazari-Hazir and Hadi Ali Chattha, after the married couple was rearrested on terrorism-related charges just hours after the Supreme Court granted them bail on September 17.The Office of the UN high commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) said that the latest charges relate to an earlier case dating back to March 2025, when the two lawyers were accused in connection with their participation in a protest that authorities deemed illegal.The UN experts said they had already expressed concern over the couple’s conviction in a separate case involving social media posts in which they supported local activists and criticised the military.They said the decision to invoke an older case immediately after Mazari-Hazir and Chattha secured bail “appears to be an attempt” to use the criminal justice system to punish freedom of expression and human rights advocacy.The couple’s rearrest was followed by proceedings before an Islamabad anti-terrorism court. Police had sought 30 days of custody for interrogation, but the court rejected the request and ordered that the lawyers be sent to jail on a 14-day judicial remand, OHCHR said.Their legal proceedings continued on September 22, when an Islamabad anti-terrorism court returned their bail petitions because they did not carry signed powers of attorney, according to the UN rights office.The UN experts also raised broader concerns about Pakistan’s use of counter-terrorism legislation, criticising what they described as “vague and broad” provisions that could be used to restrict human rights and interfere with legitimate advocacy.They called on Pakistani authorities to drop any charges stemming from the lawyers’ exercise of freedom of expression or their legitimate professional work.The experts also urged authorities to ensure that the couple had access to lawyers of their choice, their families and necessary medical care.The UN experts said they had been in contact with the Pakistani government over their concerns.
Article Summary: Pakistani lawyers Imaan Mazari-Hazir and Hadi Ali Chattha were rearrested on terrorism-related charges just hours after the Supreme Court granted them bail. The UN experts said they had already expressed concern over the couple’s conviction in a separate case involving social media posts in which they supported local activists.

Article Title: Policeman killed in gunmen attack in Pakistan’s khyber pakhtunkhwa
Article Text:
A police officer was killed in Pakistan's Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.

A police officer was killed in Pakistan's Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province after two armed med riding a motorcycle attacked him with a hand grenede and fired at him while he was deployed outside a hospital, police said.The attack took place in the unstable province of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa's Tank area.The banned Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) later claimed the responsibility for the attack, as per the PTI report.According to the police, the two attackers escaped from the spot on their motorcyclen after the attackSecurity personnel have launched a search operation to trace the assailants, while an investigation into the incident is also in progress.Over the years, there have been several instances of terrorist violence in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, which shares a border with Afghanistan. The transfer of combatants across borders and subsequent military actions have also been connected to the disturbance.The TTP has continued to carry out attacks in the province since its ceasefire agreement with the Pakistani government ended in November
Article Summary: The attack took place in the unstable province of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa's Tank area. The banned Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) later claimed responsibility for the attack. Article Title: Pakistan forces kill 7 TTP militants in North Waziristan amid rising violence along Afghan border
Article Text:
Pakistan military-led government refers to the banned TTP as Fitna al Khawarij.

Seven militants belonging to the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) were killed by security forces during an intelligence-based operation in north-western Pakistan on Friday, according to an official.The operation took place in Eidak, an area of North Waziristan district in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, which has witnessed repeated militant attacks in recent years.Security forces also destroyed several hideouts during the operation, the official said. The action was carried out under the government's Azm-e-Istehkam move, which is part of Pakistan's purported efforts to tackle terrorism.Pakistan's federal government refers to the banned Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan, or TTP, as Fitna al Khawarij.Khyber Pakhtunkhwa has remained a major hotspot for militant violence, partly because of its border with Afghanistan. The region has also seen repeated military operations and the movement of fighters across the border.The TTP ended its ceasefire with the Pakistani military-led government in November 2022. Since then, the group has carried out repeated attacks in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, particularly against security forces.Figures from the Centre for Research and Security Studies show that Khyber Pakhtunkhwa was Pakistan's worst-hit region for violence in the third quarter of 2025.It recorded 638 violence-related deaths, accounting for nearly 71 per cent of the national total, along with 221 violent incidents, or more than 67 per cent of the total.Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan, both of which border Afghanistan, together accounted for more than 96 per cent of militant-related violence recorded in Pakistan during that period.Separately, Reuters sources reported an attack on a convoy of paramilitary troops in the volatile Kurram district. Roadside bombs struck the convoy before a large group of militants opened fire, according to five Pakistani security officials.The Pakistani Taliban claimed responsibility for that attack in a statement to a Reuters reporter. Pakistan's military public relations wing did not immediately respond to requests for comment.Security forces launched a search operation to locate those responsible, while the government had not issued an official statement at the time of the report.The TTP has intensified attacks on Pakistani security forces in recent months. The group seeks to overthrow the Pakistani government and establish its own hardline interpretation of Islamic rule.Islamabad has accused Afghanistan of allowing the TTP to use its territory to train fighters and plan attacks inside Pakistan. Kabul has denied the allegation.
Article Summary: Seven militants belonging to the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) were killed by security forces during an intelligence-based operation. The operation took place in Eidak, an area of North Waziristan district in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province. Security forces also destroyed several hideouts during the operation, the official said.

Article Title: Jail, isolation, crackdown: Why Pakistan’s establishment has failed to break Imran Khan
Article Text:
Former Pakistan PM Imran Khan has been incarcerated since 2023 (File photo)

How Imran Khan got here

Why Imran Khan matters

Imran Khan: From cricket captain to PM to inmate

How state failed to marginalise Imran Khan politically

Imran Khan: PTI's 'red line'

The 'persecution' of Imran Khan

Main legal cases against Imran Khan

Imran Khan: A case that resonates beyond politics

The state’s struggle to marginalise Imran Khan

Islamabad had prepared for another confrontation. Roads were blocked, security forces deployed and Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) supporters were expected to march towards the capital demanding the release of their jailed leader, Imran Khan Then, days before the September 27 protest, PTI postponed the march until October 4, temporarily easing the pressure on the government.But the roads can be reopened and the barricades removed. The political problem surrounding Imran Khan is proving harder to clear.The former prime minister has now spent more than three years behind bars. The establishment has used imprisonment, restrictions on his contact with the outside world, scores of legal cases and a crackdown on his supporters. Yet none of it has so far succeeded in removing Imran Khan from the centre of Pakistan's politics. PTI-backed independents won the largest number of directly elected national assembly seats in the 2024 general election, and his supporters continue to mobilise around demands for his release.The postponed Islamabad march is therefore less an end to the latest confrontation than another pause in a political standoff that has survived elections, convictions and imprisonment.Imran Khan retired from international cricket in 1992, shortly after leading Pakistan to its first and, so far, only 50-over Cricket World Cup title. Four years later, in 1996, he formally entered politics by founding the PTI.His political breakthrough finally came after the 2018 general election, when the PTI emerged as the single-largest party and he became prime minister. His rise to power was widely seen by rivals and analysts as having benefited from the backing of Pakistan’s military, the country’s most powerful institution, although both Khan and the military denied that the army had helped bring him to power.That relationship subsequently deteriorated. In April 2022, the opposition brought a parliamentary no-confidence vote against Imran Khan, which he lost and was thus removed from office.He has since faced more than 100 cases, many involving corruption allegations. Several of his convictions have been overturned, suspended or otherwise challenged, while he has consistently denied wrongdoing.Imran Khan was imprisoned in August 2023 and has remained behind bars since then. Yet his incarceration has done little to diminish his presence in Pakistan’s public life or erase him from the public consciousness.Thanks to his cricket career, Imran Khan was already a well-known public figure before entering politics. Following his retirement, he gained further goodwill by giving Pakistan its first specialised cancer hospital, the Shaukat Khanum Memorial Cancer Hospital, named after his mother, in Lahore. The hospital opened in 1994.That personal following later became the foundation of a political movement, the PTI, that presented him as an outsider challenging Pakistan’s established political order. In a country where civilian politics has long been shaped by the Bhutto-Zardari and Sharif families, Imran Khan offered voters a figure outside the traditional political dynasties. His image as a retired cricket captain with no family legacy in politics helped distinguish him from the established political class.His prime ministership brought him further visibility and established him as a central figure in Pakistan’s civilian politics.And therein lies his significance: an outsider who challenged Pakistan’s established political dynasties, became prime minister, and later fell out with the military establishment before being jailed.Pakistan’s 2024 general election offered the clearest indication that Imran Khan’s imprisonment had not erased his political relevance. Despite the PTI being stripped of its election symbol and Imran Khan remaining in prison, PTI-backed independents won 92 directly elected National Assembly seats — more than candidates backed by any other political grouping.While that result did not bring the party back to power, it showed that his absence from the ballot did not translate into the disappearance of his support.However, the outcome should not have been a surprise. In October 2022, just months after his ouster as prime minister, Imran Khan contested by-elections in seven of eight National Assembly constituencies voting on October 16. He won six of the seven seats he contested, while the Pakistan People’s Party won the other two constituencies.He then won another by-election in Kurram on October 30, taking his tally of by-election victories that month to seven.The by-election results offered an early indication that removing Imran Khan from office had not dented his electoral support. The 2024 elections reinforced that point, showing that his imprisonment and the restrictions placed on the PTI had not eliminated its support among voters.As its founder and most prominent face, PTI has repeatedly described Imran Khan as its “red line.” The phrase took on greater significance after his arrest on May 9, 2023, when Pakistan witnessed widespread rioting and arson by PTI supporters. Protesters targeted government buildings and military installations, including the residence of a corps commander in Lahore and the army’s general headquarters in Rawalpindi.The events marked a dramatic escalation in the confrontation between Imran Khan and the military establishment. They also demonstrated why the PTI has continued to place him at the centre of its politics: attempts to remove him from the political arena have not removed the attachment to him among a significant section of the party’s supporters.Since his incarceration, the party has repeatedly mobilised in Islamabad, demanding his release. The federal government’s frustration with these protests was evident ahead of the recently postponed Islamabad march, when interior minister Mohsin Naqvi spoke of the need to find a “permanent solution” to the PTI’s repeated demonstrations in the capital.“This time we will find a permanent solution; we will not leave it halfway,” Naqvi said.Therefore, Imran Khan remains the PTI’s “red line” — one reason efforts to marginalise him politically have so far struggled to succeed.Imran Khan’s prolonged imprisonment has also strengthened a persecution narrative around him. His party and supporters have consistently argued that the numerous cases against him are politically motivated and intended to keep him out of politics. Pakistani authorities have rejected those allegations.The fact that more than 100 cases have been brought against him, his disqualification by the Election Commission in 2022, and the restrictions imposed on the PTI ahead of the 2024 general elections have only strengthened that narrative among his supporters.The conditions of his imprisonment at Rawalpindi’s Adiala Jail have added another dimension to the persecution narrative.In December 2025, UN Special Rapporteur on torture Alice Jill Edwards raised concerns over reports that Khan was being held in conditions falling below international standards for humane and dignified detention. The communication cited allegations of prolonged solitary confinement, restricted access to the outside world and inadequate ventilation.Edwards subsequently urged Pakistani authorities to end his reported solitary confinement and ensure that his detention conditions complied with international standards, warning that the reported conditions could amount to torture or other inhuman or degrading treatment.The Pakistani establishment has succeeded in keeping Imran Khan behind bars. But with so many eyes on his case, it has not succeeded in making his political relevance disappear.The controversy surrounding Imran Khan’s imprisonment has increasingly extended beyond politics and Pakistan, as his cricketing legacy has kept his case in the international spotlight.Former international cricket captains have appealed to Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif’s government over Khan’s treatment and access to medical care. In August, 21 former captains urged the government to ensure “humane treatment and proper medical care” for their former on-field rival.Matters almost came to a head during the recent England-Pakistan Test series. During the second Test at Lord’s, the Pakistan Cricket Board reportedly considered not sending its players back onto the field after the lunch break after Sky Sports aired an interview with Imran Khan’s sons, Kasim and Suleiman.The PCB ultimately returned to the field and lodged a complaint with the broadcaster.The episode underscored how Imran Khan’s imprisonment continues to attract attention beyond Pakistan and outside politics.Every time the PTI has marched on Islamabad, the Pakistan government has responded by fortifying the capital, blocking entry routes and deploying thousands of police and paramilitary personnel.Ahead of the September 27 march, authorities deployed thousands of security personnel and erected extensive barricades and roadblocks around Islamabad.The crackdown extended to Imran Khan’s family too, with his three sisters detained ahead of the now-postponed march.Such measures may prevent protesters from reaching Islamabad, but they have not stopped the PTI from returning to the streets with the same central demand: Imran Khan’s release. The state has managed to contain individual protests, but each confrontation has been followed by another, keeping his imprisonment at the centre of Pakistan’s politics.By isolating him in prison and cracking down on his family and party, the Pakistani authorities have sought to contain Imran Khan’s political influence. So far, however, his electoral support, PTI’s continued mobilisation and the attention surrounding his imprisonment show that those measures have not removed him from the country’s political contest.For now, Imran Khan’s ability to retain political relevance despite his imprisonment remains a significant feature of Pakistan’s politics.
Article Summary: Former Pakistan PM Imran Khan has been incarcerated since 2023. He has faced more than 100 cases, many involving corruption allegations. Several of his convictions have been overturned, suspended or otherwise challenged. Yet none of it has so far succeeded in removing Imran Khan from the centre of Pakistan's politics.

India hits back at Pakistan’s Kashmir references

UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres on Tuesday avoided directly responding to a Pakistani journalist’s question on UN Security Council resolutions on Jammu and Kashmir , instead highlighting what he described as a crisis of legitimacy and effectiveness within the council.Guterres was speaking at a joint press conference in Pakistan with deputy prime minister and foreign minister Ishaq Dar during his three-day official visit to the country.When asked about the Security Council’s resolutions on Jammu and Kashmir , Guterres said, “I have the opinion that all problems can be solved by peace and dialogue, and my good offices are always available for all situations.”He then turned to the need for reform of the UN Security Council.“The question of the Security Council is simple, Security Council does not represent the world of today. Just to give an example, we have three European members in the Security Council and no African member in the Security Council, I mean permanent members, which means that the Security Council has a problem of legitimacy and has a problem of effectiveness,” he said.Guterres also criticised the role of powerful countries in conflicts and called for stronger multilateral action to uphold international law.“We are witnessing today a situation in which superpowers, permanent members of the Security Council, are the first to start conflicts, and sometimes violating international law, creates a situation in which many countries believe they can do whatever they want because nothing will happen to them, and we see that around the world,” he said.He added, “And this is something that can only be solved with a reform of the Security Council that makes it more legitimate, but also with the capacity of the countries that have more responsibilities in the world to understand that when the principles of law are at stake, they must unite to make sure that they are fully implemented.”The remarks came as India separately responded to Pakistan’s references to Jammu and Kashmir at the 153rd assembly of the Inter-Parliamentary Union in Arusha, Tanzania.Rajya Sabha deputy chairman Harivansh exercised India’s right of reply and criticised Pakistan for raising the Kashmir issue at the international parliamentary forum.“Honourable Chairperson, we deplore the attempts by a delegation to politicise the forum and to bring in unwarranted references to issues which do not fall within the purview of this forum or meeting,” Harivansh said.He added, “Quite habitually, this delegation attempts to indulge in propaganda and makes baseless allegations against India. The Union territories of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh have been, are, and shall always remain integral and inalienable parts of India.”India's response came against the backdrop of its stated position on terrorism and tensions with Pakistan following the April 22, 2025, Pahalgam terror attack, in which 26 people were killed. India subsequently launched Operation Sindoor against terror infrastructure and training facilities in Pakistan and Pakistan-occupied Jammu and Kashmir.The two countries later engaged in military hostilities before a ceasefire was reached. India has also said that the three terrorists involved in the Pahalgam attack were subsequently killed during Operation Mahadev.
Article Summary: UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres avoided directly responding to a Pakistani journalist’s question on UN Security Council resolutions on Jammu and Kashmir. He instead highlighted what he described as a crisis of legitimacy and effectiveness within the council. He was speaking at a joint press conference in Pakistan during his three-day official visit to the country.

Article Title: 'Tarique hasn't ruled out India visit': Dhaka
Article Text:
Bangladesh PM Tarique Rahman

DHAKA: PM Tarique Rahman has "not ruled out" a visit to India through a proper bilateral framework, Dhaka said Monday, stressing New Delhi must prevent individuals based in India from using its territory to make political statements or engage in activities aimed at destabilising Bangladesh."Restraining an extremist in their land is not too much to ask," state minister for foreign affairs Humaiun Kobir said, a reference to a past news conference of former Bangladesh PM Sheikh Hasina. Bangladesh would not allow anyone from India to use Bangladeshi territory to make statements against India, he told reporters."To maintain relations with another country, bilateral engagement is required. We will do it directly. The (PM's) visit will be bilateral, and we will talk," he said. "We must address the challenge of trust. Without trust, partnerships weaken," Kobir said.
Article Summary: Bangladesh PM Tarique Rahman has "not ruled out" a visit to India through a proper bilateral framework. Rahman stresses New Delhi must prevent individuals based in India from using its territory to make political statements or engage in activities aimed at destabilising Bangladesh.

Article Title: Nepal ends flood search with over 5,000 still missing, including 189 Indians
Article Text:
File photo: A drone view of mud-covered properties following the flash flood at Trishuli in Nuwakot district, Nepal (Picture credit: Reuters)

Nepal on Monday suspended all non-essential search and rescue operations 40 days after the Aug 26 Bhotekoshi-Trishuli floods, which left 1,455 people dead and 5,285 missing. It is now shifting focus to reconstruction and rehabilitation.Those still unaccounted for include 189 Indians and dozens of people of Indian origin holding foreign passports.The decision was taken at a meeting of National Council for Disaster Risk Reduction and Management, chaired by PM Balendra Shah. It followed recommendations from district disaster management committees, National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) and teams that inspected flood-hit areas.The council recommended that the finance ministry approve Nepalese Rs 559 billion (Rs 35,000 crore) for 504 reconstruction and rehabilitation programmes submitted by ministries and agencies, with NDRRMA tasked with seeking additional funds for projects whose costs were yet to be assessed.Latest data from Nepal's tourism department showed 606 foreign tourists from 36 countries missing. Indians formed the largest group at 189, followed by 65 Americans, 55 Malaysians, 54 Ukrainians, 37 Chinese, 33 each from Australia and Latvia, 32 British nationals and 30 Canadians.Another 188 Nepalese tourists were also missing.Separately compiled figures from Indian states showed 85 missing from Tamil Nadu, 37 from West Bengal, 30 from Gujarat, 25 from Telangana, 22 from UP, 13 each from Karnataka and Andhra, 12 from Bihar, over 10 from Maharashtra and four from Odisha.
Article Summary: Nepal on Monday suspended all non-essential search and rescue operations 40 days after the Aug 26 Bhotekoshi-Trishuli floods. It is now shifting focus to reconstruction and rehabilitation. Those still unaccounted for include 189 Indians and dozens of people of Indian origin holding foreign passports.
